items.name: Magnesium (any form)
items.metricText: Time to fall asleep; deep sleep
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: About 5 min faster to fall asleep in people who were low in magnesium; near zero in everyone else. Deep sleep does not move.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: Small trials found people fell asleep about 15 minutes faster, mostly older adults or people who were low in magnesium to begin with. The effect on deep sleep and other stages is small or absent.
items.goalNotes: Goal sleep: Tier 1. Goal cramps or 'general': Tier 3. Dose under 200 mg elemental: Tier 2 (dose too low).
items.question: Which form, and how much a day?
items.answerOptionsText: glycinate · citrate · malate · threonate · oxide · spray or oil · not sure; dose in mg elemental
items.ruleText: form = oxide or spray → Tier 2 (form not absorbed). form = glycinate, citrate, malate, threonate AND dose under 200 mg elemental → Tier 2 (dose too low). Otherwise goal sleep → Tier 3 (effect too small, can run anyway); goal cramps or general → Tier 3.
items.safety: Loose stools at high doses. Kidney disease: ask a clinician first.
items.dayOne: Where it worked in trials, the change was a few minutes, mostly in people low in magnesium. That's about a third of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.

items.name: Magnesium spray / oil (transdermal)
items.effectBasis: Tier 2; not absorbed.
items.evidence: No controlled study has shown that magnesium gets through skin in a meaningful amount. The one small trial claiming it did wasn't blinded, meaning people knew what they were getting.
items.goalNotes: Always Tier 2.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: There's no evidence magnesium gets through skin in a meaningful amount. If the ritual is part of your wind-down, that's real and it's yours. The $15 a month for the magnesium itself isn't doing anything.
items.factCheckNotes: That no controlled study shows skin absorption. Look for: Gröber 2017 review of transdermal magnesium.

items.name: Melatonin
items.usualGoal: time to fall asleep, jet lag
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: About 7 min faster to fall asleep against a 10-min swing, so 0.7 for most people. Use 1.2 if the person takes over 30 min to fall asleep or has a shifted schedule (that's who it works for).
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.lowestDoseText: 0.3 mg is already active; more is not better
items.evidence: Reviews that pool many trials say it helps people fall asleep about 7 minutes faster and sleep about 8 minutes longer. It works well for jet lag and shifted schedules, less well for ordinary trouble sleeping. Taking more than 1 mg adds grogginess, not effect.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1. If dose > 5 mg, verdict adds the 'less is more' line.
items.question: Which form, and how much a day?
items.answerOptionsText: 0.3 · 0.5 · 1 · 3 · 5 · 10 mg; gummy or tablet
items.ruleText: No tier flip. dose over 1 mg → verdict adds the 'less is more' line. dose over 5 mg → safety note.
items.safety: Gummy doses are often mislabeled. Ask a clinician before nightly long-term use, for teens, or in pregnancy.
items.dayOne: Testable. The interesting question isn't whether it works, it's whether you need it every night or only when your schedule shifts.
items.factCheckNotes: 7 and 8 minute figures. Look for: Ferracioli-Oda 2013 meta-analysis.

items.name: Ashwagandha (KSM-66 / Sensoril)

items.testDesign: 2 weeks on, 2 weeks off (not this semester)
items.effectBasis: Modest sleep and HRV changes after 6 to 8 weeks. Long blocks only.
items.evidence: Several trials lasting 6 to 8 weeks found people said they felt less stressed and slept a bit better. The effect builds over weeks, not nights.
items.goalNotes: Slow: long blocks only. v1: honest 'can't test in 14 days' plus evidence line. Dose under 250 mg: Tier 2 (dose too low).
items.question: Which form, and how much a day?
items.answerOptionsText: KSM-66 · Sensoril · other extract · plain root powder · not sure; dose in mg
items.ruleText: form = plain root powder under 1 g, or extract under 250 mg → Tier 2 (dose too low). Otherwise Tier 1, queued (slow).
items.safety: Rare liver injury reports; can raise thyroid hormone. Avoid in pregnancy. Stop and ask a clinician if you get nausea or dark urine.
items.dayOne: This one works slowly, so a two-week on/off test would be unfair to it. We'll tell you what the trials found, and queue it for a longer test when we can run one.
items.factCheckNotes: Liver injury and thyroid reports. Look for: LiverTox (NIH) entry on ashwagandha.

items.name: THC / cannabis for sleep
items.testDesign: stop once, wait a week, then compare
items.effectBasis: 15 min faster to fall asleep and a clear REM drop, but the catch-up effect on stopping breaks the 3/3 test. Special design only.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: It helps you fall asleep faster in the short term and cuts down REM sleep. When you stop, you get several nights of REM catch-up and worse sleep. That catch-up effect makes a simple on/off test give the wrong answer.
items.goalNotes: Not alternation-compatible (rebound). v1: report evidence only. Later: single switch with 7-night washout.
items.question: How many nights a week, usually?
items.answerOptionsText: 0 · 1 to 2 · 3 to 4 · 5 or more. Asked plainly, no comment, no follow-up.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.safety: Legal status varies. Nightly use builds tolerance; withdrawal insomnia is real and temporary.
items.dayOne: We can't run this as a 3-on/3-off test, because the off nights after nightly use are worse for everyone, and that would make the cannabis look like it 'works'. That would be a dishonest result, so we won't give you one.
items.factCheckNotes: REM suppression and rebound. Look for: Babson 2017 review.

items.name: Vitamin D3
items.evidence: Clearly useful if you're low in it, which is common in winter and for people with darker skin living far from the equator. In people whose levels are normal, large trials found little benefit for mood, energy or catching fewer colds.

items.dayOne: We can't see this in your data, and we won't tell you to drop it, because if you're low it matters. A blood level costs about $30 and answers this properly.
items.factCheckNotes: Large trials in non-deficient people. Look for: VITAL (Manson 2019); D-Health (Neale 2022).

items.goalNotes: Goal omega-3: Tier 2 (form not absorbed). As a food, fine.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Your body converts very little of this into the omega-3s fish oil provides. Fine as a food, not as a substitute.
items.factCheckNotes: ALA to EPA/DHA conversion under 10%. Look for: Burdge & Calder 2005.

items.name: Creatine monohydrate
items.evidence: One of the best-supported supplements there is for strength and muscle in people who train. There's growing evidence it helps thinking when you're short on sleep.
items.goalNotes: Dose under 2 g: Tier 2 (dose too low). Otherwise Tier 3 with 'strong evidence, keep if you lift'. Never Tier 1: saturation takes weeks, so alternation is invalid.
items.question: Which form, and how much a day?
items.answerOptionsText: monohydrate · HCl · buffered · blend; g a day
items.ruleText: dose under 2 g a day → Tier 2 (dose too low). form = HCl, buffered, or 'creatine blend' → verdict notes monohydrate is the studied form. Otherwise Tier 3 keep.
items.safety: Take with water; a small water-weight gain is normal. Fine for kidneys in healthy adults.
items.dayOne: We can't see this in sleep or HRV, and that's fine, because the evidence here is strong. If you lift, keep it. If you don't, it's mostly doing nothing.
items.factCheckNotes: 3 g minimum. Look for: ISSN position stand (Kreider 2017).

items.name: Protein powder
items.evidence: It's food. Useful if you don't get enough protein from meals, irrelevant if you do.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 (food). Verdict shows cost.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: No flip.
items.dayOne: This is food, not a supplement, so there's no verdict to give. If it helps you hit protein, keep it. If you already eat enough, it's an expensive way to buy calories.

items.name: BCAAs
items.evidence: If you eat enough protein, BCAAs add nothing, and that's been tested several times. They're already in the protein you eat.
items.goalNotes: Tier 2 (tested, found nothing).
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: These are already in every protein source you eat. Trials in people eating enough protein show nothing extra. Easy $25 back.
items.factCheckNotes: That BCAAs add nothing with adequate protein. Look for: Wolfe 2017 JISSN review.

items.name: Glutamine
items.evidence: Found nothing for recovery in healthy adults. The gut evidence is from hospital patients only.
items.goalNotes: Goal gut with a diagnosed condition: Protected. Otherwise Tier 2.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Useful in hospitals, not in healthy people. This one can go.
items.factCheckNotes: No recovery benefit in healthy adults. Look for: Gleeson 2008 review.

items.name: Beta-alanine
items.evidence: Reliably helps with hard efforts lasting 1 to 4 minutes. Does nothing for longer or shorter efforts. The tingling it causes is harmless.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3: keep for rowing / 800 m / CrossFit-type efforts, otherwise verdict says it's not for your training.
items.question: Which form, and how much a day?
items.answerOptionsText: g a day
items.ruleText: dose under 2 g a day → Tier 2 (dose too low). Otherwise Tier 3, with the 1-to-4-minute note.
items.dayOne: Works, but only for hard efforts of one to four minutes. If that's your sport, keep it. If you run long or lift heavy, it isn't doing anything for you.

items.name: Pre-workout
items.metricText: Time to fall asleep; total sleep
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: As caffeine after 2pm, if taken after 1pm.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: The caffeine in it works. Most of the other ingredients are in amounts too small to matter. Taken after 2pm, it costs you sleep.
items.goalNotes: Used after 1pm: Tier 1 as caffeine timing. Otherwise Tier 3.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: If you take this after lunch, it's a caffeine-timing experiment, and one of the most reliable ones we run.

items.name: Electrolytes (LMNT etc.)
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: No sleep effect to expect.
items.evidence: Useful if you sweat heavily or eat very low-carb. For a normal day, plain water does the same and the extra sodium isn't helpful.
items.goalNotes: Trains over 1 h/day or keto: Tier 3 keep. Otherwise Tier 3 with 'water does this'. Goal sleep: Tier 1.
items.question: How many times in the last 30 days?
items.answerOptionsText: training sessions over an hour, per week
items.ruleText: Training over an hour a day, or keto → Tier 3 keep. Otherwise Tier 3 with 'water does this'. Fires the frequency question for training, not for the product.
items.safety: High blood pressure: a gram of sodium a day on top of diet is not trivial.
items.dayOne: If you're sweating hard for an hour a day, this earns its place. If you're not, water does the same job, and this is mostly salt and flavour at $45 a month.

items.name: Greens powder (AG1 etc.)
items.evidence: There are no independent studies of the product. It's a low-dose multivitamin plus a blend of ingredients whose amounts aren't disclosed.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 (untestable). Verdict shows annual cost prominently.
items.question: Still paying for it?
items.answerOptionsText: Yes · no · not sure. Prefilled from the subscriptions list where the person connected one.
items.ruleText: still paying = yes → Tier 3 with annual cost. Overlap group 'daily multivitamin' → overlap check.
items.dayOne: We can't measure this one and neither has anyone else; there are no independent trials. What we can show you is that it's over a thousand dollars a year. That's the whole verdict, and the call is yours.
items.factCheckNotes: No independent trials. Search PubMed for the brand; note funding of anything found.

items.name: Collagen peptides
items.evidence: Several trials found small improvements in skin elasticity and joint pain after 8 to 12 weeks at 10 to 15 g a day. Many of those trials were paid for by the companies that sell it.
items.goalNotes: Dose under 5 g: Tier 2 (dose too low). Otherwise Tier 3 with skin/joint rating.
items.question: Which form, and how much a day?
items.answerOptionsText: g a day (a scoop is usually 10 g)
items.ruleText: dose under 5 g a day → Tier 2 (dose too low). 5 to 10 g → Tier 3 with 'below the studied dose'. 10 g or more → Tier 3 with skin/joint rating.
items.dayOne: Invisible to a ring, and the trials that found something used 10 grams for two months. If you want to know, a daily one-tap skin or joint rating over eight weeks is the honest way.
items.factCheckNotes: 10 to 15 g trials and their funding. Look for: de Miranda 2021 meta-analysis (note sponsor declarations).

items.name: Biotin
items.evidence: It only helps if you're deficient, and almost nobody is. It also interferes with common blood tests, including thyroid and heart tests.
items.goalNotes: Tier 2 (tested, found nothing). Safety note always shown.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.safety: Tell your doctor you take it before any blood test; it can distort results.
items.dayOne: Unless you're deficient, which almost nobody is, this doesn't grow hair. And it can throw off blood tests, which is a real reason to stop, not just a financial one.
items.factCheckNotes: No hair benefit without deficiency; lab-test interference. Look for: Patel 2017 review; FDA 2017/2019 biotin interference safety communication.

items.name: Hyaluronic acid (oral)
items.evidence: Small trials for skin hydration and knee pain. The effects are modest.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 with rating.
items.question: Which form, and how much a day?
items.answerOptionsText: mg
items.ruleText: dose under 120 mg → Tier 2 (dose too low). Otherwise Tier 3 with skin rating.
items.dayOne: Can't see it; small trials say maybe. A daily skin rating for eight weeks is the test.

items.name: Turmeric / curcumin
items.evidence: Decent trials for knee arthritis pain, but only with forms designed to be absorbed. Plain turmeric powder in a capsule is barely absorbed at all.
items.goalNotes: Plain turmeric powder: Tier 2 (form not absorbed). Formulated curcumin with joint goal: Tier 3 with pain rating.
items.question: Which form, and how much a day?
items.answerOptionsText: plain turmeric · curcumin with piperine · phytosome / Meriva · other; mg
items.ruleText: form = plain turmeric powder or spice capsule → Tier 2 (form not absorbed). form = curcumin with piperine, phytosome, or micellar → Tier 3 with pain rating.
items.safety: Blood thinners, gallstones: check.
items.dayOne: If the label says 'turmeric' without a form designed to be absorbed, almost none of it is absorbed. If it's a proper curcumin, we can't see it in your data but a pain rating can.

items.name: Glucosamine / chondroitin
items.evidence: The large trials mostly found nothing. People with moderate to severe knee pain may get some relief.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 with pain rating.
items.question: Which form, and how much a day?
items.answerOptionsText: mg a day
items.ruleText: dose under 1,000 mg a day → Tier 2 (dose too low). Otherwise Tier 3 with pain rating.
items.dayOne: The big trials were mostly disappointing. If your knees say otherwise, a daily rating will show it.

items.name: CoQ10
items.evidence: Helps with muscle aches caused by statin drugs, and in some heart conditions. It does nothing for energy in healthy adults.
items.goalNotes: On a statin: Tier 3 keep. Otherwise Tier 3 with 'not for energy in healthy people'.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Real use if you're on a statin and achy. As a general energy supplement, the evidence isn't there.

items.name: NMN / NR
items.evidence: It raises a molecule called NAD in the blood. No human trial has shown that this changes any health outcome you'd notice. The living-longer data is from mice.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 (untestable). Annual cost shown.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: No flip. Cost shown.
items.dayOne: This raises a blood marker; nobody has shown it changes anything you'd notice. We can't test a longevity claim on you, and neither can anyone else. $840 a year, and it's your bet to make.
items.factCheckNotes: No human outcome trials. Look for: Yoshino 2021 (NMN, no clinical outcome change).

items.name: Resveratrol
items.evidence: Poorly absorbed, and human trials found no benefit for the heart or for blood sugar.
items.goalNotes: Tier 2 (tested, found nothing).
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: The human trials came back flat, and it barely absorbs anyway. This one can go.
items.factCheckNotes: Human trials found no heart or blood-sugar benefit. Look for: Cochrane review on resveratrol for cardiovascular outcomes; Berman 2017.

items.name: Lion's mane
items.evidence: One small trial in older adults with early memory problems. Nothing in healthy adults.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 with focus rating.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: The evidence is one small study in a very different group. A daily focus rating for a month is a fairer test than that study.

items.name: Rhodiola
items.testDesign: 2 weeks on, 2 weeks off (not this semester)
items.effectBasis: Weak trials, slow.
items.evidence: Some trials for tiredness, but they aren't well run.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 with energy rating.
items.question: Which form, and how much a day?
items.answerOptionsText: mg a day
items.ruleText: dose under 200 mg a day → Tier 2 (dose too low). Otherwise Tier 3 with energy rating.
items.dayOne: Can't see it in the ring. An energy rating over a few weeks can.

items.name: Ginkgo biloba
items.evidence: Large trials in healthy adults, and trials trying to prevent memory loss, found nothing.
items.goalNotes: Tier 2 (tested, found nothing).
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.safety: Blood thinners: interaction.
items.dayOne: This was tested properly, at scale, and it didn't do anything for memory. One of the clearest 'no' answers in the whole supplement aisle.
items.factCheckNotes: Large trials found nothing. Look for: GEM study (DeKosky 2008, JAMA); Laws 2012 meta-analysis in healthy adults.

items.name: Saffron
items.evidence: Small trials have found, fairly consistently, that it helps with low mood, in some cases about as much as a low dose of antidepressant.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 with mood rating. Diagnosed depression: Protected.
items.question: Which form, and how much a day?
items.answerOptionsText: mg a day
items.ruleText: dose under 30 mg a day → Tier 2 (dose too low). Otherwise Tier 3 with mood rating.
items.dayOne: Better evidence than its price tag suggests. We can't see mood in your sleep data, so a daily mood tap is the test.
items.factCheckNotes: Mood trials. Look for: Lopresti 2014 review.

items.name: Phosphatidylserine
items.effectBasis: Old, mixed, small.
items.evidence: A few small, old trials with mixed results.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Thin evidence, and we can't see it. Your call on whether $30 a month is worth the maybe.

items.name: Zinc (daily)
items.evidence: Zinc lozenges taken at the first sign of a cold shorten it slightly. Taking zinc every day when you're not low in it does nothing, and more than 40 mg a day drains your copper.
items.goalNotes: Daily use with no deficiency: Tier 2. Lozenges at cold onset: Tier 3 keep.
items.question: Which form, and how much a day?
items.answerOptionsText: mg; daily · lozenges when ill
items.ruleText: dose over 40 mg a day → safety note (copper). Daily use with no deficiency → Tier 2 (tested, found nothing). Lozenges only at cold onset → Tier 3 keep.
items.safety: Over 40 mg a day long term causes copper deficiency.
items.dayOne: Daily zinc without a deficiency doesn't do the things it's sold for, and too much of it causes its own problem. Keep lozenges for the first day of a cold; drop the daily.
items.factCheckNotes: Copper depletion above 40 mg/day; daily zinc no benefit without deficiency. Look for: NIH ODS zinc fact sheet (tolerable upper limit 40 mg).

items.name: Vitamin C (daily)
items.evidence: It doesn't stop you catching colds. It makes them about 8 percent shorter. Cheap and harmless.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3, no push.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: No flip.
items.dayOne: Doesn't prevent colds, shortens them by about half a day. It's $8. Not worth an experiment or a fuss either way.
items.factCheckNotes: 8% figure. Look for: Hemilä 2013, Cochrane.

items.name: Elderberry
items.evidence: Small trials suggested shorter colds. The biggest and best-run trial found nothing.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: No flip.
items.dayOne: Evidence is small and the best trial was flat. Can't measure it either way.
items.factCheckNotes: Largest trial null. Look for: Macknin 2020.

items.name: Probiotic (generic daily)
items.evidence: Whether a probiotic helps depends on the exact strain and the exact problem. A generic daily capsule for a healthy gut has little evidence behind it.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 with gut rating.
items.question: Which form, and how much a day?
items.answerOptionsText: named strain · generic blend · not sure
items.ruleText: form = named strain for a named problem (e.g. Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG for antibiotic diarrhoea) → Tier 3 keep. form = generic blend or 'not sure' → Tier 3 with gut rating.
items.dayOne: Probiotics are specific tools for specific problems. A generic daily one for general gut health has less behind it than the shelf suggests. A gut rating over a month is the honest test.

items.name: Psyllium / fibre
items.evidence: Well supported for regularity and LDL.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 keep.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Not exciting, and very well proven. Keep.

items.name: Digestive enzymes
items.evidence: No benefit unless a doctor has found you're missing a specific enzyme. The exception is lactase, if dairy upsets your stomach.
items.goalNotes: Lactase for lactose intolerance: Tier 3 keep. Otherwise Tier 3 with 'thin evidence' and gut rating.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Unless it's lactase and you're lactose intolerant, there isn't much behind these. A gut rating on and off is a fair test.

items.name: Apple cider vinegar
items.evidence: One small trial on weight, and a small effect on blood sugar after meals. It wears away tooth enamel.
items.goalNotes: Goal weight: Tier 2. Goal glucose: Tier 3 (CGM only).
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.safety: Dilute it; it damages enamel.
items.dayOne: For weight, the evidence is one small trial. For your teeth, the evidence is clear. This can go.
items.factCheckNotes: Weight trial size and enamel erosion. Look for: Khezri 2018 (n=39); dental erosion case reports.

items.name: Berberine
items.evidence: Lowers blood sugar in people whose blood sugar is high. Calling it 'natural Ozempic' oversells it a lot. It interacts with many medications.
items.goalNotes: Diabetes / prediabetes / on medication: Protected. Otherwise Tier 3.
items.question: Which form, and how much a day?
items.answerOptionsText: mg per dose, doses a day
items.ruleText: dose under 1 g a day → Tier 2 (dose too low). Any medication, diabetes, or prediabetes → Protected.
items.safety: Interacts with metformin, statins, blood thinners and more. Ask a clinician.
items.dayOne: This does something real, which is exactly why it isn't an app decision. If you're on any medication, please run it past whoever prescribes them.
items.factCheckNotes: Interaction list. Look for: NIH / LiverTox; CYP interactions.

items.name: Green tea extract (EGCG)
items.evidence: A tiny effect on weight. Concentrated extracts have caused liver damage at high doses.
items.goalNotes: Tier 2 with safety note.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.safety: Concentrated extracts have caused liver injury. Tea is fine; capsules are not risk-free.
items.dayOne: The weight effect is close to zero and the liver risk isn't. Drink the tea instead.
items.factCheckNotes: Weight effect and liver injury reports. Look for: Cochrane review (Jurgens 2012); Hu 2018 hepatotoxicity review.

items.name: Fat burner / thermogenic
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Resting heart rate up about 3 bpm from the stimulants. A test would show the cost, not a benefit.
items.evidence: Mostly caffeine and other stimulants. They don't burn fat in any amount you'd notice, and they do raise your heart rate and disturb your sleep.
items.goalNotes: Tier 2 (tested, found nothing) with safety note. Optional Tier 1 to show the resting heart rate/sleep cost.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.safety: Stimulant blends raise heart rate and blood pressure.
items.dayOne: These don't burn fat in any amount you'd notice, and they do raise your resting heart rate. We can show you that number if you want, but the verdict is already in.
items.factCheckNotes: No fat loss beyond caffeine; heart rate and blood pressure effects. Look for: Jeukendrup & Randell 2011 review.

items.name: Testosterone booster (tribulus, fenugreek, D-AA)
items.evidence: Tribulus and D-aspartic acid have been tested and found not to raise testosterone. Fenugreek has a tiny effect on sex drive and none on testosterone.
items.goalNotes: Tier 2. Diagnosed low T: Protected.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Tested, repeatedly, and they don't raise testosterone. If you're worried about your levels, that's a blood test and a doctor, not a bottle.
items.factCheckNotes: Null results for tribulus and D-AA. Look for: Qureshi 2014 tribulus review; Willoughby & Leutholtz 2013 D-AA trial.

items.name: Tongkat ali
items.evidence: A few small trials with modest results. Nobody outside the original team has repeated them.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Thin, not nothing. We can't see it, so this one is a judgement call with the price in front of you.

items.name: Maca
items.evidence: Small trials suggest a little help with sex drive. No change in hormones.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 with rating.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Small evidence for libido, none for hormones. A rating is the only way to know.

items.name: DHEA / pregnenolone
items.evidence: These are hormones. They're not something to experiment with on your own.
items.goalNotes: Always Protected.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.safety: Hormone precursors: prescriber only.
items.dayOne: This is a hormone. We don't route hormones, and we'd gently suggest a doctor does.

items.name: Taurine
items.evidence: The longevity claim is from a 2023 mouse study. Human outcome data doesn't exist.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: The headline study was in mice. There's nothing to see in your data and nothing yet in humans. At $12 it isn't costing you much, but it isn't doing much either.

items.name: Activated charcoal
items.evidence: There's no 'detox' for it to do. It soaks up whatever is in your gut, including your medications and vitamins.
items.goalNotes: Tier 2 with safety note.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.safety: Binds medications, including the pill. Don't take near any medication.
items.dayOne: There's nothing for it to detox, and it will absorb your medications and vitamins along with everything else. This one can go.
items.factCheckNotes: No detox mechanism; binds medications. Look for: any toxicology text; NHS / FDA guidance on charcoal and drug absorption.

items.name: Sea moss
items.evidence: No human trials. The amount of iodine in it varies wildly and can be far too much.
items.goalNotes: Tier 2 with safety note.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.safety: Iodine excess can disturb thyroid function.
items.dayOne: No trials, unpredictable iodine, and the claims come from social media. Yours to keep, but we'd rather you knew.
items.factCheckNotes: No human trials; iodine variability. Look for: iodine content analyses of seaweed products; NIH iodine upper limit.

items.name: Shilajit
items.evidence: One small trial paid for by the seller. Raw shilajit has repeatedly been found to contain lead and arsenic.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 with safety note.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.safety: Buy only tested products; raw shilajit has contained lead and arsenic.
items.dayOne: Can't see it, thin evidence, and the safety note matters more than the verdict.

items.name: Chlorophyll water
items.evidence: TikTok origin. No trials.
items.goalNotes: Tier 2.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: There are no studies of this at all. The claims came from social media, and there's nothing here for us to test. Yours to keep, but we'd rather you knew.
items.factCheckNotes: No human trials for the skin / detox claims.

items.name: Colostrum
items.evidence: Some evidence it helps endurance athletes with gut problems during hard training. The general wellness claims haven't been tested.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 with gut rating; annual cost shown.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Some evidence in endurance athletes, none for the general claims. $600 a year for a maybe. Your call.

items.name: Mushroom coffee
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: About a third of normal coffee's caffeine.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: The mushroom part has no human evidence at these doses. It's coffee with less caffeine.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 for the mushroom claim. Tier 1 as caffeine timing if after 1pm.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: The mushrooms aren't doing anything we or anyone else can measure. The 'fewer jitters' is just less caffeine. A smaller cup of ordinary coffee gets you the same thing for a lot less.

items.name: Nootropic stack (alpha-GPC etc.)
items.evidence: Taken one ingredient at a time, the evidence is small. Nobody has tested the stacks as products.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 with focus rating. Contains caffeine after 1pm: Tier 1.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: A focus rating on and off is the only honest test. Two weeks, one tap a day.

items.name: Inositol
items.evidence: Decent evidence for PCOS. That's a medical use.
items.goalNotes: PCOS: Protected. Otherwise Tier 3.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: If this is for PCOS, it's between you and your clinician, and we stay out of it.

items.name: Vitamin K2
items.evidence: Makes sense biologically. The trials that measured actual health outcomes are small and mixed.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.safety: Warfarin: do not take without prescriber.
items.dayOne: Plausible, unproven, invisible to us. Keep it if the logic convinces you; the trials haven't settled it.

items.name: Calcium
items.evidence: Useful if you don't get much from food. Taking more than you need may slightly raise heart risk.
items.goalNotes: Doctor-sourced: Protected. Otherwise Tier 3 with 'food first'.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Food first for this one. If a doctor asked you to take it, keep taking it.

items.name: Evening primrose oil
items.evidence: Careful reviews of all the trials found it works no better than a sugar pill for PMS or eczema.
items.goalNotes: Tier 2.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Reviewed properly and it didn't beat placebo. This can go.
items.factCheckNotes: No better than placebo for PMS or eczema. Look for: Cochrane review (Bamford 2013) for eczema; Whelan 2009 for PMS.

items.name: Coffee after 2pm
items.metricText: Total sleep; time to fall asleep; deep sleep
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: About 41 min less total sleep in the classic trial, against a typical 45-min swing. Bigger for people who drink a lot; smaller for fast caffeine metabolisers.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: In the classic trial, 400 mg of caffeine taken six hours before bed cut sleep by about 41 minutes, and people didn't notice. Caffeine takes 5 to 6 hours for half of it to clear, and that varies a lot from person to person.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1. Best first experiment for most users.
items.question: What time, usually?
items.answerOptionsText: before noon · 12 to 2pm · 2 to 5pm · after 5pm. Prefilled from Oura or WHOOP caffeine tags where present.
items.ruleText: last coffee before noon → not a hypothesis; Tier 3 'not an issue for you'. 12 to 2pm → Tier 1 with a smaller expected effect (0.6, so gated to Tier 3 unless they choose to run it). After 2pm → Tier 1.
items.dayOne: The single most reliable experiment we run, and the one most people are wrong about in one direction or the other. Fourteen days and you'll have your own number.
items.factCheckNotes: The 41-minute figure and 6-hour timing. Look for: Drake 2013, J Clin Sleep Med.

items.name: Second (or third) coffee
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Each extra cup after the first adds a modest, inconsistent amount. Only clear when the second cup is late.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: Total daily caffeine above about 400 mg is where sleep and HRV effects become consistent.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1: on = usual, off = cap at one.
items.question: How many times in the last 30 days?
items.answerOptionsText: cups a day: 1 · 2 · 3 · 4+
items.ruleText: cups a day = 1 → not a hypothesis. 2 → Tier 3 (effect too small). 3 or more → Tier 1 (expected effect 0.8).
items.dayOne: The second cup usually makes a smaller difference than the timing of the last one. That's about two fifths of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.

items.name: Energy drinks
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Caffeine effect plus a small resting-heart-rate rise from sugar and taurine. Clearer if drunk after 2pm; use 1.0 then.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: Caffeine plus sugar. Same sleep cost as coffee with more effect on resting heart rate.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1.
items.question: What time, usually?
items.answerOptionsText: before noon · 12 to 2pm · after 2pm
items.ruleText: after 2pm → Tier 1 (effect 1.0). Before 2pm → Tier 3 (effect too small). Observe-only either way.
items.dayOne: Unless you drink these late in the day, the effect on a single night is modest. That's about two thirds of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.

items.name: Decaf swap after noon
items.metricText: Time to fall asleep; total sleep
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: The caffeine experiment in reverse. Same size as 'coffee after 2pm'.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: The inverse of the caffeine experiment. Keeps the ritual, drops the drug.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Offered as the 'off' condition for the coffee experiment; not routed on its own.
items.dayOne: Keeps the cup, drops the caffeine. A clean test of whether it was ever the caffeine.

items.name: Matcha / green tea in the afternoon
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: About a third of the caffeine of coffee, so about a third of the effect.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: Less caffeine than coffee, plus theanine. Still caffeine.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1 if after 2pm.
items.question: What time, usually?
items.answerOptionsText: before 2pm · after 2pm
items.ruleText: after 2pm → Tier 3 (effect too small, can run anyway). Before → not a hypothesis.
items.dayOne: There's about a third as much caffeine here as in coffee. That's about two fifths of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.

items.name: Alcohol in the evening
items.metricText: Overnight HRV; resting heart rate; REM; time awake during the night
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: HRV down 10 to 25% and resting heart rate up 3 to 5 bpm on every wearable's own data. The largest, most reliable effect in the whole table.
items.historyText: partly: the night has a recognisable pattern we can flag for them to confirm
items.evidence: Even one or two drinks lower overnight HRV (the recovery number) by 10 to 25 percent and raise resting heart rate by a few beats. You fall asleep faster and then sleep worse in the second half of the night. It shows up the same night on every wearable.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1. Frame as 'what does a drink cost you', never as 'stop drinking'.
items.question: How many nights a week, usually?
items.answerOptionsText: 0 · 1 to 2 · 3 to 4 · 5 or more
items.ruleText: 0 → not in the inventory. 1 to 2 → Tier 1, observe-only, expected effect 1.5 but fewer on-nights, so the test runs over 3 to 4 weeks. 3 or more → Tier 1, observe-only, two weeks is enough.
items.safety: If drinking feels hard to change, that's a conversation for a person, not an app.
items.dayOne: We're not going to tell you not to drink. We're going to show you what one drink costs you the next morning, in your own numbers, and let you decide what it's worth on a Tuesday.
items.factCheckNotes: HRV 10 to 25% and resting heart rate 3 to 5 bpm figures. Look for: WHOOP and Oura published member data; Pietilä 2018 (Firstbeat).

items.name: Late dinner (within 2–3 h of bed)
items.metricText: Time to fall asleep; time awake during the night; resting heart rate
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Resting heart rate up 1 to 2 bpm overnight; sleep changes are small. Bigger for heavy meals; use 0.8 if the person eats their main meal within 90 min of bed.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: Eating close to bedtime raises your heart rate and body temperature overnight. The effect on sleep is modest and varies a lot between people.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1.
items.question: What time, usually?
items.answerOptionsText: hours between dinner and bed: under 1.5 · 1.5 to 3 · over 3
items.ruleText: main meal within 90 min of bed → expected effect 0.8, Tier 1. 90 min to 3 h → Tier 3 (effect too small). Over 3 h → not a hypothesis.
items.dayOne: Eating late nudges your overnight heart rate up a little. That's about half of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.

items.name: Big carbohydrate dinner
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: One small trial, about 5 min faster to fall asleep.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: In one small trial, a high-carb meal about 4 hours before bed helped people fall asleep faster. Sugar right before bed does the opposite.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: One small trial found a few minutes' difference. That's about two fifths of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.

items.name: Dessert / sugar before bed
items.metricText: Time awake during the night; deep sleep
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Lighter sleep in studies that watched people; no controlled trial.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: Associated with lighter sleep in studies that watched people rather than tested them.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: The studies here only watched people; nobody has run a proper test. That's about a third of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.

items.name: Fasting window / skipping breakfast
items.testDesign: 2 weeks on, 2 weeks off (not this semester)
items.effectBasis: Small, mixed effects on sleep and resting heart rate. Slow to settle, so long blocks only.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: For weight, it works about as well as any other way of eating less. Its effects on sleep and HRV are small and vary between people. Your body takes about a week to adjust, so 3-day blocks are too short to test it fairly.
items.goalNotes: Slow: long blocks only. v1: evidence line.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.safety: Not for anyone with a history of disordered eating.
items.dayOne: This changes your body over a week, not a night, so we can't test it fairly in three-day blocks yet. What we can tell you: for weight it works about as well as any other way of eating less.

items.name: Fluids after 8pm
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: About 8 fewer minutes awake for people who wake to use the bathroom; near zero for people who don't. Use 1.0 if the person reports night bathroom trips.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: Needing the bathroom is the most common reason people wake in the middle of the night. Cutting fluids after 8pm reduces it.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1.
items.question: How many times in the last 30 days?
items.answerOptionsText: bathroom wake-ups a week: 0 · 1 to 2 · 3+
items.ruleText: wakes for the bathroom most nights → expected effect 1.0, Tier 1. Rarely → Tier 3 (effect too small).
items.dayOne: If you don't wake up needing the bathroom, this one probably isn't costing you anything. That's about three fifths of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.
items.factCheckNotes: Nocturia as the top cause of waking. Look for: any urology review of nocturia prevalence.

items.name: Nicotine pouches / vape
items.metricText: Time to fall asleep; overnight HRV; resting heart rate
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Stimulant: resting heart rate up, HRV down, on nights with evening use. Similar in size to late caffeine.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: Nicotine is a stimulant. It raises resting heart rate, lowers HRV (the recovery number), and breaks up sleep. Using it in the evening is the worst for sleep.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1: test evening use only (on = as usual, off = none after 6pm). Never frame as a quit programme.
items.question: What time, usually?
items.answerOptionsText: daytime only · some after 6pm · mostly evening
items.ruleText: any use after 6pm → Tier 1 (evening timing test, observe-only). Daytime only → Tier 3 (not a sleep hypothesis).
items.safety: Dependence is real and quitting is hard. We test evening timing, not abstinence.
items.dayOne: We won't lecture you. We'll test just the evening ones and show you what they cost your sleep. What you do with that is yours.
items.factCheckNotes: Nicotine and sleep. Look for: Jaehne 2009 review.

items.name: Kombucha / probiotic drinks
items.evidence: It has hardly been tested as a health drink at all.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 with gut rating; cost shown.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Untested, and $40 a month. A gut rating on and off is the only test that exists.

items.name: Bone broth
items.evidence: A modest protein source. The collagen claims don't survive digestion any better than collagen powder.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: This is a decent bowl of soup with some protein in it. The claims about skin and joints aren't backed by studies, but you don't need a verdict to enjoy soup. If it's $40 a month, that's the only thing worth looking at.

items.name: Training after 7pm
items.metricText: Time to fall asleep; total sleep; overnight HRV
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Averages near zero, but for hard sessions ending within 2 h of bed, time to fall asleep and resting heart rate move by about a full swing. Use 1.0 if the session is vigorous and late; 0.4 if it's easy or ends before 8pm.
items.historyText: yes, the wearable already records it
items.evidence: Reviews that pool many studies say evening exercise doesn't harm sleep on average, but vigorous exercise within an hour of bed delays it. Individual variation is large.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1. On = usual late session, off = same session before 7pm or in the morning.
items.question: What time, usually?
items.answerOptionsText: (read from workouts)
items.ruleText: Read from the wearable's workout times; not asked. Vigorous session ending within 2 h of bed on 3+ nights a week → expected effect 1.0, Tier 1. Easy sessions, or ending before 8pm → Tier 3 (effect too small).
items.dayOne: On average, evening training is fine for sleep. But you're not an average, and this is one of the things that varies most from person to person. Worth a real test.
items.factCheckNotes: Averages versus late-vigorous subgroup. Look for: Stutz 2019 meta-analysis, Sports Med.

items.name: Morning workout before 8am
items.metricText: Time to fall asleep; deep sleep
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Small body-clock nudge over days.
items.historyText: yes, the wearable already records it
items.evidence: Exercising in the morning nudges your body clock a little earlier.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: The body-clock nudge from morning exercise is real but small night to night. That's about a third of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.

items.name: HIIT in the evening
items.metricText: Time to fall asleep; overnight HRV; resting heart rate
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Resting heart rate and body temperature stay up into the night after hard intervals close to bed.
items.historyText: yes, the wearable already records it
items.evidence: Vigorous intervals within 1–2 hours of bed raise body temperature and resting heart rate into the night.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1.
items.question: What time, usually?
items.answerOptionsText: (read from workouts)
items.ruleText: Read from workouts. Within 2 h of bed → Tier 1. Otherwise not a hypothesis.
items.dayOne: Of all the training-timing questions, this is the one most likely to show up in your sleep data. Worth the two weeks.

items.name: 10,000 steps / daily walk
items.metricText: Resting heart rate; share of time in bed actually asleep
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Resting heart rate 1 bpm lower and sleep a little more solid on active days. Real but small night to night.
items.historyText: yes, the wearable already records it
items.evidence: Being active during the day reliably improves sleep and lowers resting heart rate over time. The effect of any single day's walk on that night's sleep is real but modest.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1 (on = 8k+, off = under 5k). Verdict notes long-term benefits regardless of the night-level result.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Walking pays off over months; one day's effect on that night is small. That's about half of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.

items.name: Zone 2 cardio (3+ h/week)
items.testDesign: 2 weeks on, 2 weeks off (not this semester)
items.effectBasis: Over 8 to 12 weeks, HRV and resting heart rate move by a full swing or more. Too slow for 3-day blocks.
items.historyText: yes, the wearable already records it
items.evidence: Raises HRV (the recovery number) and lowers resting heart rate over 6 to 12 weeks. The evidence is strong. It's far too slow to test in 3-day blocks.
items.goalNotes: Long-block only. v1: evidence line plus trend view.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Works, slowly, and the evidence is about as strong as it gets. Not a two-week test; we'll show you the trend instead.
items.factCheckNotes: HRV and RHR change over weeks. Look for: Sandercock 2005 meta-analysis.

items.name: Strength training
items.testDesign: 2 weeks on, 2 weeks off (not this semester)
items.historyText: yes, the wearable already records it
items.evidence: Strong evidence for almost everything you could want. It's not something that changes a single night's sleep, so it isn't a candidate for a two-week test.
items.goalNotes: Not routed for testing. Verdict: keep.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Not something we'd ever suggest testing away. Keep.

items.name: Stretching / yoga before bed
items.metricText: Time to fall asleep; overnight HRV
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: About 5 min faster to fall asleep in small trials.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: Small trials found gentle evening yoga helped people fall asleep faster.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: The small trials found a few minutes' difference in falling asleep. That's about two fifths of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.

items.name: Cold plunge / ice bath
items.metricText: Overnight HRV; resting heart rate; time to fall asleep (if evening)
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Acute HRV changes are real but go both ways; evening plunges can delay sleep. Direction is the interesting part, so a test is still worth it if the person is choosing whether to buy one.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: It does change HRV and alertness in the short term. The recovery benefits are modest, and doing it right after lifting weights actually reduces muscle growth. An evening plunge can make it harder to fall asleep.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1. Pre-purchase proxy: cold shower for 14 days.
items.question: What time, usually?
items.answerOptionsText: morning · evening
items.ruleText: evening → number = time to fall asleep. Morning → number = overnight HRV. Either way Tier 3 (effect too small, can run anyway); pre-purchase proxy offered.
items.safety: Cold shock is a real cardiac stressor. Ease in, never alone.
items.dayOne: The overnight effect is small and goes both ways from person to person. That's about half of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.
items.factCheckNotes: Blunted muscle growth after lifting. Look for: Roberts 2015, J Physiol.

items.name: Cold shower (morning)
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Alertness is real; overnight numbers barely move.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: One trial found people took fewer sick days, though they got ill just as often. The jolt of alertness is real, even though it's a feeling rather than a number.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1. Also the free proxy for a plunge purchase.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: The jolt is real. The overnight numbers barely notice. That's about a third of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.

items.name: Sauna (post-workout or evening)
items.metricText: Overnight HRV; resting heart rate; time to fall asleep
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Falling asleep about 10 min faster after an evening session, against a 10-min swing.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: Long-term studies of large groups in Finland link frequent sauna use to fewer deaths from heart disease, though that's from watching people over years, not a controlled test. An evening sauna helps many people fall asleep faster, because body temperature drops afterwards.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1. Pre-purchase proxy: hot bath or shower 1–2 h before bed.
items.question: What time, usually?
items.answerOptionsText: morning · midday · evening
items.ruleText: evening sessions → number = time to fall asleep, Tier 1. Morning or midday → number = overnight HRV, expected effect 0.5, Tier 3 (effect too small).
items.safety: Hydrate. Not with alcohol.
items.dayOne: The long-term heart evidence is from watching people rather than testing them but consistent. The sleep effect is testable tonight. Both facts belong in your file.
items.factCheckNotes: Finnish cohort. Look for: Laukkanen 2015, JAMA Intern Med.

items.name: Hot bath / shower 1–2 h before bed
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: About 10 min faster to fall asleep in a review of 17 studies, against a 10-min swing.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: A review that pooled 17 studies found people fell asleep about 10 minutes faster when they had a warm bath or shower 1 to 2 hours before bed.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1. Free. Also the proxy for sauna.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Tier 1. Also the stand-in test for a sauna purchase.
items.dayOne: One of the best-supported free sleep tools there is, and the one we'd test before you buy a sauna.
items.factCheckNotes: 10-minute figure. Look for: Haghayegh 2019, Sleep Medicine Reviews.

items.name: Breathwork (box, 4-7-8, physiological sigh)
items.metricText: Overnight HRV; time to fall asleep
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Big effect on HRV during the exercise; the part that carries into overnight HRV is modest.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: Slow breathing reliably raises HRV (the recovery number) acutely. A 2023 trial found 5 minutes a day of exhale-focused breathing beat mindfulness for mood.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Slow breathing lifts HRV while you do it; less carries into the night. That's about half of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.

items.name: Meditation app (Calm, Headspace)
items.metricText: Time to fall asleep; overnight HRV
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Measured sleep changes are small, though people say they sleep better.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: Good evidence that people feel less stressed and say they sleep better. The measured changes in sleep are smaller.
items.goalNotes: Goal sleep: Tier 1. Goal stress: Tier 3 (stress rating).
items.question: When did you last use it?
items.answerOptionsText: This week · this month · 1 to 3 months ago · longer · can't remember. 'Can't remember' is treated as 'longer'.
items.ruleText: last used over 30 days ago AND still paying → Tier 2 (not being used). Used this month → Tier 3 (effect too small, can run anyway). Overlap group 'meditation apps'.
items.dayOne: People say they sleep better; the measured change is small. That's about two fifths of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.

items.name: NSDR / yoga nidra
items.metricText: Overnight HRV; time to fall asleep
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Small trials; relaxation is real, overnight change is small.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: Small trials. Acute relaxation effects are real.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: The relaxation is real; the measured change on the night is small. That's about a third of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.

items.name: Journaling / worry list before bed
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: About 9 min faster to fall asleep in the lab trial, against a 10-min swing.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: In a lab trial, people who spent five minutes writing tomorrow's to-do list fell asleep about 9 minutes faster.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Tier 1.
items.dayOne: Five minutes, free, and one decent trial behind it. Easy test.
items.factCheckNotes: 9-minute figure. Look for: Scullin 2018, J Exp Psychol Gen.

items.name: Gratitude practice
items.effectBasis: A wearable can't see mood.
items.evidence: A modest benefit for mood in trials. A wearable can't see it.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 with mood rating. Free: verdict says keep if it helps.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Can't see it, costs nothing, evidence says it helps a little. Keep it if it's yours.

items.name: Reading (paper) before bed
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Mostly measures what it replaces (a screen).
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: Small trials versus screens favour paper.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.

items.name: Screens / phone in bed
items.metricText: Time to fall asleep; total sleep
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: 20 to 30 min later to fall asleep with social media in bed, against a 10-min swing on time to fall asleep and a 45-min swing on total sleep. Bigger for heavy users.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: What you're looking at, and how worked up it gets you, matters more than the blue light. People who use social media in bed fall asleep 20 to 30 minutes later, in studies that watched people rather than tested them.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1: off = phone charges outside the bedroom.
items.question: How many times in the last 30 days?
items.answerOptionsText: nights a week with the phone in bed: 0 to 2 · 3 to 5 · most
items.ruleText: most nights → Tier 1. Rarely → not a hypothesis.
items.dayOne: The most-tested free change there is, and the one nobody actually tests on themselves. Three nights at a time, phone in the kitchen.
items.factCheckNotes: 20 to 30 min figure. Look for: Levenson 2017; Exelmans & Van den Bulck 2016.

items.name: Work email after 9pm
items.metricText: Time to fall asleep; overnight HRV
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Later to fall asleep and lower HRV in studies that watched people; no controlled trial.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: People who do work late into the evening tend to fall asleep later and have lower HRV (the recovery number).
items.goalNotes: Tier 1.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.

That's about half of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.

items.metricText: Time to fall asleep; total sleep
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Shorter, lighter sleep in studies that watched people.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: Falling asleep to TV is associated with shorter, lighter sleep.

items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.

That's about half of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.

items.name: Consistent wake time (±30 min)
items.metricText: Share of time in bed actually asleep; time to fall asleep
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Share of time asleep up 3 to 5 points and easier to fall asleep once the clock settles. Builds over the first week.
items.historyText: yes, the wearable already records it
items.evidence: A 2023 study that followed 60,000 people found that keeping a regular sleep schedule predicted living longer better than how many hours people slept. It's the single strongest sleep habit we know of.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1 (on = fixed wake time including weekends, off = free). Verdict leans keep regardless.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: (read from sleep data)
items.ruleText: Read from sleep data: wake-time spread over the last 30 days. Spread over 60 min → Tier 1. Under 30 min → already doing it; 'kept' on day one.
items.dayOne: If there's one thing to keep no matter what your two weeks say, it's this. We'll still show you the number.
items.factCheckNotes: 60,000-person regularity study. Look for: Windred 2024, Sleep (UK Biobank).

items.name: Weekend sleep-in (over 1 h)
items.metricText: Time to fall asleep Sunday/Monday; share of time in bed actually asleep
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Sunday night 20 to 40 min later to fall asleep, but it's one night a week, which dilutes the average. Use weekly blocks.
items.historyText: yes, the wearable already records it
items.evidence: Sleeping in by an hour or two at the weekend shifts your body clock later, which makes Sunday night harder and Monday morning worse.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1 (weekly blocks).
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: (read from sleep data)
items.ruleText: Read from sleep data. Weekend wake time over 60 min later than weekday → Tier 3 (effect too small, weekly blocks offered).
items.dayOne: The Sunday-night effect is real, but it's one night a week. That's about two thirds of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.
items.factCheckNotes: Social jet lag. Look for: Wittmann 2006.

items.name: Afternoon nap (after 3pm or over 30 min)
items.metricText: Time to fall asleep; total night sleep
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: 10 to 15 min longer to fall asleep on nap days for people who nap late. Near zero for short early naps.
items.historyText: yes, the wearable already records it
items.evidence: Short, early naps are fine. Late or long naps use up some of the tiredness you need to fall asleep at night.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1.
items.question: What time, usually?
items.answerOptionsText: (read from wearable)
items.ruleText: Read from the wearable where it detects naps. Naps after 3pm or over 30 min on 3+ days a week → Tier 1. Otherwise not a hypothesis.
items.dayOne: Naps aren't the enemy. Late long naps might be. Testable.
items.factCheckNotes: Late naps and night sleep. Look for: Milner & Cote 2009 review.

items.name: Snoozing the alarm
items.metricText: Share of time in bed actually asleep
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: The 2023 trial found essentially nothing.
items.evidence: A 2023 trial found that 30 minutes of snoozing didn't do any harm, and slightly helped people think clearly in the morning, at least for people who snooze regularly.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1. Low priority.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: The 2023 trial found essentially nothing either way. That's about a fifth of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.
items.factCheckNotes: 2023 snooze trial. Look for: Sundelin 2023, J Sleep Res.

items.name: Checking the sleep score every morning
items.effectBasis: Not testable with the device that causes it.
items.evidence: Sleep-score anxiety is a documented thing: for some people, worrying about the number makes their sleep worse.
items.goalNotes: Not testable with the device that causes it. Verdict: gentle note plus option to hide scores.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: We're aware of the irony. If checking your score makes you anxious, we can hide it and just send verdicts. Say the word.

items.name: Morning sunlight (10 min outdoors)
items.metricText: Time to fall asleep; total sleep
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: 5 to 10 min earlier to fall asleep after a week. Builds slowly; weekly blocks.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: Morning light nudges your body clock earlier, which helps you get sleepy earlier at night. The effect builds up over several days.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1 with 7/7 blocks preferred.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: This builds over a week or more, which makes it hard to see in short blocks. That's about half of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.
items.factCheckNotes: Body-clock advance. Look for: Wright 2013, Curr Biol.

items.name: Grounding / earthing (sheets, mats)
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Tier 2; no mechanism.
items.evidence: The trials are tiny, the people in them knew what they were getting, and most were run by people selling the products. There's no known way for it to work.
items.goalNotes: Sheets/mats: Tier 2. Barefoot walking: Tier 3 (it's a walk; walks are good).
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: The walk is good for you. The 'earthing' part has no mechanism and no real trials. Keep the walk, skip the $30 sheet.
items.factCheckNotes: That trials are small, unblinded and proponent-run. Look for: Chevalier 2012 (author affiliations).

items.name: Weighted blanket
items.metricText: Time to fall asleep; time awake during the night
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: People say it helps a lot; measured changes are about 5 min on falling asleep and staying asleep.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: A proper controlled trial in people with insomnia and mental health conditions found they said it helped a lot. The measured changes in their sleep were smaller than what they reported.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1.
items.question: When did you last use it?
items.answerOptionsText: This week · this month · 1 to 3 months ago · longer · can't remember. 'Can't remember' is treated as 'longer'.
items.ruleText: last used over 30 days ago → Tier 2 (not being used). In use → Tier 3 (effect too small, can run anyway).
items.dayOne: People say it helps a lot; the measured change is a few minutes. That's about half of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.
items.factCheckNotes: The trial and its population. Look for: Ekholm 2020, J Clin Sleep Med.

items.name: Mouth tape
items.metricText: Share of time in bed actually asleep; breathing rate; time awake during the night
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: No measured effect in people without snoring. Use 0.8 if the person or partner reports snoring.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: One small trial in people with mild sleep apnoea (breathing pausing during sleep) found less snoring. There are no studies in people who sleep normally.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1 with safety gate: gasping/choking or suspected apnoea: Protected plus 'see a sleep clinician'.
items.question: When did you last use it?
items.answerOptionsText: still using; snoring: yes · no · not sure
items.ruleText: last used over 30 days ago → Tier 2 (not being used). Snores or partner reports snoring → expected effect 0.8, Tier 1 with safety gate. Otherwise Tier 3.
items.safety: Don't tape if you can't breathe comfortably through your nose, or if you suspect sleep apnoea (breathing stopping during sleep).
items.dayOne: Unless you snore, there's no measured effect to look for. That's about a third of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.
items.factCheckNotes: The one small apnoea trial. Look for: Lee 2022, Healthcare (mouth taping in mild OSA).

items.name: Nasal strips / dilator
items.metricText: Breathing rate; time awake during the night; share of time in bed actually asleep

items.name: Blue-light blocking glasses

items.name: Eye mask

items.effectBasis: Modest gain in darkness unless the room is already dark.

items.name: Light therapy box (10,000 lux)
items.typicalAmount: 20–30 min, morning (purchase price spread over 24 months)

items.name: Red light therapy panel
items.typicalAmount: 10 min daily (purchase price spread over 24 months)

items.answerOptionsText: This week · this month · 1 to 3 months ago · longer · can't remember. 'Can't remember' is treated as 'longer'.

items.name: Eight Sleep / cooling mattress pad
items.typicalAmount: nightly (subscription plus purchase price spread over 24 months)

items.name: Continuous glucose monitor (no diabetes)

items.name: Humidifier

items.answerOptionsText: This week · this month · 1 to 3 months ago · longer · can't remember. 'Can't remember' is treated as 'longer'.
