items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Nothing here to test. This one can go without any experiment at all.
items.factCheckNotes: No mechanism; FTC actions against sellers.

items.name: Hydrogen / alkaline water
items.evidence: Alkaline water is neutralised by stomach acid. Hydrogen water has small trial paid for by the sellers only.
items.goalNotes: Tier 2.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Your stomach acid undoes alkaline water on contact. Hydrogen water has a couple of tiny company trials. Tap water and $40 back.
items.factCheckNotes: Stomach acid neutralises alkaline water; hydrogen water trials are small and seller-funded.

items.name: Vibration plate
items.evidence: Some evidence for bone strength in older adults. The fat-loss claims have no support.
items.goalNotes: Goal fat loss: Tier 2. Goal bone: Tier 3.
items.question: When did you last use it?
items.answerOptionsText: This week · this month · 1 to 3 months ago · longer · can't remember. 'Can't remember' is treated as 'longer'.
items.ruleText: unused for 30 days → Tier 2 (not being used). Goal fat loss → Tier 2 (tested, found nothing). Goal bone → Tier 3.
items.dayOne: For fat loss, no. For bone density in older adults, some evidence. Depends why you bought it.

items.name: LED face mask
items.evidence: Reasonable evidence that red and near-infrared light helps with wrinkles and acne if you use it consistently.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 with skin rating.
items.question: When did you last use it?
items.answerOptionsText: This week · this month · 1 to 3 months ago · longer · can't remember. 'Can't remember' is treated as 'longer'.
items.ruleText: unused for 30 days → Tier 2 (not being used). Otherwise Tier 3 with skin rating. Overlap group 'at-home skin devices'.
items.dayOne: Decent evidence and we can't see skin. A daily skin rating over eight weeks is the way.

items.name: Jaw exerciser
items.evidence: No evidence. TMJ risk.
items.goalNotes: Tier 2 with safety note.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Tier 2 (no way it could work) with safety note.
items.safety: Can cause jaw joint problems.
items.dayOne: No evidence it does what it claims, and dentists warn it can cause jaw problems. This one is safe to skip.
items.factCheckNotes: TMJ risk. Look for: dental association statements on jaw exercisers.

items.name: Water filter
items.evidence: Sensible if your tap water has known issues. Otherwise taste.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 keep.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: There's nothing to test here. If your tap water has known problems, it's sensible. If not, it's about taste. Keep it.

items.name: Smart lights (warm, dim in the evening)
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: About 8 min earlier to fall asleep when evening light is dimmed.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: Bright evening light suppresses melatonin. Dimming helps your body clock.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Tier 3 (effect too small, can run anyway).
items.dayOne: Dimming the lights helps, but the change is under one night's normal swing. That's about two thirds of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.
items.factCheckNotes: Evening light and melatonin. Look for: Gooley 2011.

items.name: Sauna / bathhouse membership
items.metricText: Overnight HRV; time to fall asleep
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Same as sauna.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: Same evidence as sauna above. The membership just makes it a cost question.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1 as sauna. Pre-purchase proxy: hot bath.
items.question: How many times in the last 30 days?
items.answerOptionsText: 0 · 1 to 3 · 4 to 7 · 8 or more. For memberships, the app can prefill this from calendar or check-in data where connected.
items.ruleText: Under 2 visits a month → Tier 2 (not being used). Otherwise Tier 1 as sauna. Overlap group 'heat and cold'.
items.dayOne: Testable, and $1,800 a year makes it worth testing.

items.name: Cryotherapy sessions
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Small overnight HRV change.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: People feel more recovered afterwards, but the measured evidence for faster recovery is weak. Standing in a cold chamber has not been shown to beat an ordinary ice bath.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1.
items.question: How many times in the last 30 days?
items.answerOptionsText: 0 · 1 to 3 · 4 to 7 · 8 or more. For memberships, the app can prefill this from calendar or check-in data where connected.
items.ruleText: No visits in 60 days but package unused → Tier 2 (not being used). Otherwise Tier 3 (effect too small, can run anyway). Overlap group 'heat and cold'.
items.dayOne: The overnight HRV change is small. That's about two fifths of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.

items.name: IV vitamin drips
items.evidence: No better than swallowing the same vitamins or drinking a glass of water, unless you're seriously dehydrated or can't absorb things through your gut.
items.goalNotes: Tier 2.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Tier 2 (tested, found nothing).
items.safety: Any injection carries infection risk. Some clinics are poorly regulated.
items.dayOne: There's no version of this that beats a glass of water and a cheap multivitamin for someone who isn't in a hospital. $3,000 a year back.
items.factCheckNotes: No benefit over oral for non-deficient people. Look for: any review of IV vitamin therapy in healthy adults; FDA warnings about compounding.

items.name: Massage (monthly)
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: HRV up for a few hours; small by the next morning.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: Reliably makes people feel less stressed and less sore. HRV goes up for a while afterwards. There's no lasting physical effect.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 with stress rating. Optional Tier 1 on HRV that night.
items.question: How many times in the last 30 days?
items.answerOptionsText: 0 · 1 to 3 · 4 to 7 · 8 or more. For memberships, the app can prefill this from calendar or check-in data where connected.
items.ruleText: Credits banked and unused for 60 days → Tier 2 (not being used). Otherwise Tier 3 with stress rating. Overlap group 'massage'.
items.dayOne: It works on how you feel and that's a real outcome. We can also check whether your HRV notices that night, if you're curious.

items.name: Facials (monthly)
items.evidence: Skin looks and feels better for a short while. There's no lasting change.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 with skin rating; cost shown.
items.question: How many times in the last 30 days?
items.answerOptionsText: 0 · 1 to 3 · 4 to 7 · 8 or more. For memberships, the app can prefill this from calendar or check-in data where connected.
items.ruleText: No visit in 90 days but still paying → Tier 2 (not being used). Otherwise Tier 3 with skin rating. Overlap group 'professional skin treatments'.
items.dayOne: We can't see your skin and we won't pretend to. $1,800 a year, and a skin rating on the weeks with and without is the honest test.

items.name: Acupuncture
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Sleep trials are weak.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: Modest evidence for chronic pain. Sleep trials are not very well run.
items.goalNotes: Goal pain: Tier 3 rating. Goal sleep: Tier 1.
items.question: How many times in the last 30 days?
items.answerOptionsText: 0 · 1 to 3 · 4 to 7 · 8 or more. For memberships, the app can prefill this from calendar or check-in data where connected.
items.ruleText: No visit in 90 days → dropped from the count. Otherwise by goal.
items.dayOne: If it's for pain, a daily pain rating is the honest test, because a ring can't see pain. If it's for sleep, we can test that directly.

items.name: Chiropractor (maintenance visits)
items.evidence: For low back pain, about as good as other hands-on treatments. 'Maintenance' visits when nothing hurts have no evidence behind them.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 with pain rating. No current pain: verdict notes maintenance has no evidence.
items.question: How many times in the last 30 days?
items.answerOptionsText: current pain: yes · no
items.ruleText: Visits with no current pain → Tier 3 with the 'maintenance has no evidence' note. Pain → Tier 3 with pain rating.
items.dayOne: If your back hurts, it's a reasonable option among several. If it doesn't, 'maintenance' isn't a thing the evidence recognises.

items.name: Physical therapy
items.evidence: Clinical care.
items.goalNotes: Protected.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Clinical, and not ours to rate. Keep going.

items.name: Therapy / counselling
items.evidence: Not a wellness item, and never put through the router.
items.goalNotes: Protected. Counted in cost only if the user wants it counted.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: This isn't a habit and we'll never put a verdict on it. If you'd rather it didn't appear in the total at all, tap to hide it.

items.name: Personal trainer
items.evidence: Turning up, and getting pushed a bit harder each time. Strong evidence that this works, if you'd otherwise skip.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 keep.
items.question: How many times in the last 30 days?
items.answerOptionsText: 0 · 1 to 3 · 4 to 7 · 8 or more. For memberships, the app can prefill this from calendar or check-in data where connected.
items.ruleText: Fewer than 2 sessions a month for two months → Tier 3 with cost per session (not a drop; the point is whether they go). Otherwise keep.
items.dayOne: Not something to test away. Keep.

items.name: Nutritionist / dietitian
items.evidence: Helps people actually stick to a plan. If it's for a medical condition, it's clinical care.
items.goalNotes: Protected.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Protected.
items.dayOne: Clinical territory. We stay out.

items.name: Gym membership
items.testDesign: 2 weeks on, 2 weeks off (not this semester)
items.historyText: yes, the wearable already records it
items.evidence: The only thing that varies is whether you go.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3: verdict shows cost per visit from activity data.
items.question: How many times in the last 30 days?
items.answerOptionsText: visits in the last 30 days; prefilled from check-ins or workouts where connected
items.ruleText: 8+ visits a month → Tier 3 keep. 4 to 7 → Tier 3 with cost per visit. Under 4 for two months running → Tier 2 (not being used). Overlap group 'fitness memberships'.
items.dayOne: The only verdict here is cost per visit. We'll compute it from your activity data and let you look at it.

items.name: Yoga / pilates studio
items.metricText: Overnight HRV; time to fall asleep
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: As stretching / yoga.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: Decent evidence for stress and sleep. The question is the cost.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 keep. Optional Tier 1 on sleep.
items.question: How many times in the last 30 days?
items.answerOptionsText: 0 · 1 to 3 · 4 to 7 · 8 or more. For memberships, the app can prefill this from calendar or check-in data where connected.
items.ruleText: Under 4 visits a month for two months → Tier 2 (not being used). Otherwise Tier 3 keep. Overlap group 'fitness memberships'.
items.dayOne: Good for you, expensive, and the only question is whether you go. Keep if you do.

items.name: Float tank
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Small trials on relaxation.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: Small trials for anxiety and relaxation.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1 on HRV/sleep that night. Tier 3 stress rating.
items.question: How many times in the last 30 days?
items.answerOptionsText: 0 · 1 to 3 · 4 to 7 · 8 or more. For memberships, the app can prefill this from calendar or check-in data where connected.
items.ruleText: Package unused for 60 days → Tier 2 (not being used). Otherwise Tier 3.
items.dayOne: The overnight change is small. That's about two fifths of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.

items.name: Hyperbaric oxygen (wellness use)
items.evidence: It's real medicine for specific conditions like diving injuries and certain wounds. There's no evidence it does anything for general wellness or living longer.
items.goalNotes: Tier 2 unless prescribed (Protected).
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Real medicine for specific conditions, no evidence for wellness use. $3,600 a year that isn't buying what it says.
items.factCheckNotes: Approved medical uses versus wellness claims. Look for: FDA list of cleared HBOT indications.

items.name: Lymphatic drainage massage
items.evidence: Your lymph system doesn't need 'draining'. The medical version is for people with a specific swelling condition. For everyone else it's a gentle massage.
items.goalNotes: Tier 2 unless lymphoedema (Protected).
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: It's a pleasant massage with a medical name attached. If you like the massage, keep it as a massage.
items.factCheckNotes: Medical use is for lymphoedema only.

items.name: Colonic / detox cleanse
items.evidence: There's nothing to detox. Your liver and kidneys do that. The risks include upsetting the body's salt balance and injuring the bowel.
items.goalNotes: Tier 2 with safety note.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.safety: Colonics carry real risks.
items.dayOne: Your liver and kidneys already do this job. This one can go, and not just for the money.
items.factCheckNotes: Risks. Look for: Mishori 2011 review of colon cleansing harms.

items.name: Consumer DNA wellness test
items.evidence: Trials that gave people diet advice based on their genes found it worked no better than ordinary advice.
items.goalNotes: Tier 2 (one-off; note sunk cost gently).
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Already paid, so nothing to save. Just know that the diet advice it produced doesn't outperform ordinary advice in trials.
items.factCheckNotes: Gene-based diet advice no better than generic. Look for: Celis-Morales 2017 (Food4Me); Gardner 2018 (DIETFITS).

items.name: Blood panel subscription (Function etc.)
items.evidence: Genuinely useful for catching the things you might be low in: vitamin D, iron, B12. The 'longevity' framing is marketing.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 keep, especially if it resolves the vitamin D / B12 / iron questions.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: Annual physical with bloodwork also in the inventory → Tier 2 (overlaps with something else) unless the subscription tests something the physical doesn't. Overlap group 'bloodwork'.
items.dayOne: Actually useful for one thing: it answers the vitamin D, B12 and iron questions we can't. Keep it for that.

items.name: Hormone / peptide clinic (TRT, GLP-1, peptides)
items.evidence: Medical treatment.
items.goalNotes: Protected. Never routed.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Medical. Not ours.

items.name: Sleep coach (CBT-I)
items.evidence: CBT-I, a structured programme for insomnia, is the best-supported treatment for insomnia there is. A coach delivering it properly is worth a lot.
items.goalNotes: Protected if CBT-I. Otherwise Tier 3.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: If this is CBT-I, it's the best-supported sleep intervention that exists. Keep.

items.name: Stretch studio (assisted stretching)
items.evidence: It improves flexibility about as well as stretching at home. The question is the cost.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 with cost.
items.question: How many times in the last 30 days?
items.answerOptionsText: 0 · 1 to 3 · 4 to 7 · 8 or more. For memberships, the app can prefill this from calendar or check-in data where connected.
items.ruleText: Under 2 visits a month → Tier 2 (not being used). Otherwise Tier 3 with cost.
items.dayOne: It works as well as stretching at home. Whether the $150 buys you actually doing it is the real question.

items.name: Retreat / wellness weekend
items.evidence: Rest works. The specific modalities usually don't add to it.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Tier 3.
items.dayOne: The rest is what's doing the work. The specific treatments on the schedule rarely add much to it. Enjoy it for the rest.

items.name: Bedroom temperature (thermostat)
items.metricText: Deep sleep; time awake during the night; share of time in bed actually asleep
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: A 2°C change moves deep sleep and time awake by about two-thirds of a swing for the average person. Use 1.0 if the room is over 21°C or the person wakes hot.
items.evidence: A cooler room, around 18 to 20°C (65 to 68°F), improves sleep for most people. The best temperature varies from person to person.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1: on = current, off = 2°C cooler. The first environmental experiment we'd suggest.
items.question: What time, usually?
items.answerOptionsText: thermostat setting; wakes hot: yes · no
items.ruleText: Room over 21°C or wakes hot → expected effect 1.0, Tier 1. Otherwise Tier 3 (effect too small, can run anyway).
items.dayOne: Two degrees matters more if your room runs warm. That's about two thirds of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.
items.factCheckNotes: 18 to 20°C range. Look for: Okamoto-Mizuno 2012 review.

items.name: Blackout / light leak
items.metricText: Time awake during the night; share of time in bed actually asleep
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Resting heart rate about 1 bpm lower and a few fewer minutes awake with real darkness.
items.evidence: A 2022 trial found that even a dim light left on overnight raised people's heart rate during sleep and made their bodies handle sugar worse the next day.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Tier 3 (effect too small, can run anyway). Overlap with eye mask: if both, keep one.
items.dayOne: Real darkness helps, by a small amount each night. That's about three fifths of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.
items.factCheckNotes: Dim light and heart rate / glucose. Look for: Mason 2022, PNAS.

items.name: Phone charging in the bedroom
items.metricText: Time to fall asleep; time awake during the night
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Same experiment as screens in bed.
items.evidence: Proximity predicts use. Use predicts delay.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1 (same experiment as screens in bed).
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Same experiment as screens in bed; routed together.
items.dayOne: See 'phone in bed'. Charging it in the kitchen is the whole experiment.

items.name: Pet in the bed
items.metricText: Time awake during the night; share of time in bed actually asleep
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: A couple of points on share of time asleep.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: Studies using movement sensors found that a dog on the bed slightly reduces how much of the night you're actually asleep. A dog in the room makes no difference.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1 (three nights in the room, not on the bed). Gentle framing.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: The measured difference is a couple of points on how much of the night you're asleep. That's about two fifths of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.
items.factCheckNotes: Movement-sensor study. Look for: Patel 2017, Mayo Clin Proc.

items.name: Partner's snoring or schedule
items.effectBasis: Can't be assigned; see earplugs.
items.evidence: In some studies, a partner's snoring costs the other person up to an hour of sleep a night.
items.goalNotes: Not routable as an experiment. Verdict: name it, suggest earplugs (Tier 1) or a conversation.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: We can't run an experiment on another person. But if the wake-ups line up with their snoring, that's worth knowing, and earplugs are a test you can run.

items.name: Kids waking you
items.effectBasis: Not an experiment; those nights are excluded.
items.historyText: yes, the wearable already records it
items.evidence: Real, not something an app can fix, and the cause of most of your bad numbers.
items.goalNotes: Verdict: exclude those nights from experiments. Never count as 'missed'.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: We'll mark those nights and keep them out of every experiment, so nothing you test gets blamed for a toddler.

items.name: Window open / fan at night
items.metricText: Deep sleep; time awake during the night
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Small studies on bedroom CO2.
items.evidence: A closed bedroom fills up with the carbon dioxide you breathe out. Small studies link higher overnight CO2 to worse sleep.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: The bedroom-CO2 studies are small. That's about two fifths of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.

items.name: Mattress age (over 8 years)
items.evidence: Medium-firm mattresses help with back pain in trials. How old the mattress is matters less than whether it still supports you.
items.goalNotes: Pre-purchase: no proxy. Verdict: use the retailer's 100-night trial as the experiment.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: We can't test a mattress you haven't bought. Most retailers give 100 nights; that's an experiment. Use it, and check your sleep data before the return window closes.

items.name: Pillow
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Little research.
items.evidence: Neck alignment. Little sleep research.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1 (new versus old).
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: There's very little research, and no reason to expect a large change. That's about a fifth of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.

items.name: Silk pillowcase
items.evidence: No trials. It causes less friction on hair, which is plausible.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Plausible for hair, untested, cheap. Not worth an experiment or a worry.

items.name: Candles / incense in the bedroom
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.evidence: Burning anything puts fine particles into the air. The calming effect is real.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3. Note ventilation.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: The calm is real and so is the smoke. Blow it out before you sleep and keep it.

items.name: Bedroom used for work
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: Later to fall asleep when the bed means work; hard to assign for most people.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: The bed-means-sleep rule: if your brain associates the bed with work, it takes longer to switch off there.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1 if feasible.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: This one is real but hard to switch on and off, and the effect is modest. That's about half of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.

items.name: Separate bedrooms some nights
items.metricText: Time awake during the night; share of time in bed actually asleep
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.effectBasis: About 10 fewer minutes awake apart; varies a lot.
items.historyText: yes, if they've been tagging it in Oura or WHOOP
items.evidence: Measured sleep is often better apart. How well people feel they slept, and how happy they are, is often better together.
items.goalNotes: Tier 1, offered only if the user raises it.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: The measured difference is about ten minutes, and it varies a lot. That's about two thirds of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs, and if you'd still like to run it, you can, knowing that going in.

items.name: Premium gym membership (Equinox, Life Time)
items.testDesign: 2 weeks on, 2 weeks off (not this semester)
items.evidence: The only thing that varies is whether you go. Twice a week or more is worth almost any price. Less than that, and it's the most expensive habit you don't have.
items.goalNotes: 8+ visits a month: keep. 4 to 7: cost per visit shown. Under 4 for two months: Tier 2 (not being used).
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: You went 3 times last month. That's $83 a visit. Nobody's saying cancel. We're saying that's the number, and it's yours to decide what it's worth.

items.name: Boutique class membership (Barry's, SoulCycle, F45, Orangetheory)
items.testDesign: 2 weeks on, 2 weeks off (not this semester)
items.evidence: Same as any gym: it works if you go. Class formats have better attendance than open gyms, which is the honest case for paying more.
items.goalNotes: Same visit thresholds as gym. Overlap group 'fitness memberships'.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Classes get people through the door more reliably than a gym floor does, which is the real reason to pay for them. If you're going, keep. If you're not, the number is $200 a month for a good intention.

items.name: Second gym or studio membership
items.evidence: Nobody needs two. The one you go to is the one to keep.
items.goalNotes: Overlap group 'fitness memberships': the one with fewer visits in 30 days is the drop.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: You've got two memberships and last month you used one of them. Keep that one. $150 a month back, and nothing about your training changes.
items.factCheckNotes: Confirm the evidence claim in the 'what the studies found' column against one independent source.

items.name: Class pack or studio credits
items.typicalAmount: credits or class packs, price spread over 24 months
items.evidence: Unused credits are the most common wellness purchase that quietly does nothing.
items.goalNotes: last used over 60 days ago: Tier 2 (not being used). Used this month: Tier 3 keep.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: There are 7 credits on that pack and the last one was used in June. If they expire, that's money gone; if they don't, book them before buying anything else. Either way this comes off the count.
items.factCheckNotes: Confirm the evidence claim in the 'what the studies found' column against one independent source.

items.name: Fitness app subscription (Peloton app, Apple Fitness+, Ladder)
items.evidence: Works for people who use it. Most subscriptions outlive the habit by months.
items.goalNotes: last used over 30 days ago AND still paying: Tier 2 (not being used). Otherwise Tier 3 keep. Overlap group 'fitness memberships'.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Last opened six weeks ago and still billing. $25 a month back, and you can always resubscribe the week you actually want it.

items.name: Recovery studio membership (Restore, Remedy Place, Othership)
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.evidence: Sauna and cold are testable; the compression, IV and cryo add-ons are not, and mostly not supported. The evidence is the sauna's and the plunge's.
items.goalNotes: Under 3 visits a month: Tier 2 (not being used). Owns a sauna or plunge: Tier 2 (overlaps with something else). Otherwise Tier 1 as sauna / cold plunge for the parts a wearable can see.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: The sauna and the plunge in there are testable, and worth testing. The rest of the menu mostly isn't. If you're going twice a week, we'll test what we can. If you went once last month, that's $250 for one visit.

items.name: Sauna or cold-plunge studio when you own one at home
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.evidence: The one at home does the same thing.
items.goalNotes: Overlap group 'heat and cold'.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: You've got a plunge in the garage and a studio membership for the same thing. The garage one is free from here. $150 a month back.
items.factCheckNotes: Confirm the evidence claim in the 'what the studies found' column against one independent source.

items.name: Massage membership (Massage Envy, Squeeze)
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.evidence: Massage reliably makes people feel better. Memberships reliably bank credits nobody uses.
items.goalNotes: Credits banked and unused for 60 days: Tier 2 (not being used). Otherwise Tier 3 with stress rating. Overlap group 'massage'.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Three credits banked and the last visit was in July. Use them, or stop the billing until you will. Massage isn't the problem; the auto-renew is.

items.name: Meal delivery or meal-prep service
items.evidence: Works if the food gets eaten. A freezer full of unopened deliveries is the tell.
items.goalNotes: still paying AND meals skipped or thrown out most weeks: Tier 2 (not being used). Otherwise Tier 3 keep.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: If most of it gets eaten, this is a fine way to spend $400. If half of it goes in the bin, that's $200 a month on food you didn't want. You'd know which.

items.name: Nutrition or calorie app (premium)
items.evidence: Logging works while people log. Most premium subscriptions outlast the logging by months.
items.goalNotes: last opened over 30 days ago AND still paying: Tier 2 (not being used).
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Last opened in August, still billing. $15 a month back until the week you want it again.

items.name: Second meditation or sleep app
items.evidence: Two apps for the same ten minutes.
items.goalNotes: Overlap group 'meditation apps': the one opened less is the drop.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Two subscriptions for the same ten minutes a day. Keep the one you actually open. $15 a month back.
items.factCheckNotes: Confirm the evidence claim in the 'what the studies found' column against one independent source.

items.name: Annual physical with bloodwork
items.evidence: Standard care. Covers most of what a subscription blood panel covers.
items.goalNotes: Protected. Overlap group 'bloodwork' (the subscription is the one that gets checked, not this).
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Standard care. Not ours to rate.

items.name: Electrolytes plus sports drink
items.evidence: Two sources of the same salts and sugar.
items.goalNotes: Overlap group 'electrolytes': the sports drink is the drop.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: You're buying salt and sugar twice. Keep the packets if you sweat hard; the sports drink is the same thing with more sugar. $40 a month back.
items.factCheckNotes: Confirm the evidence claim in the 'what the studies found' column against one independent source.

items.name: Collagen drinks and beauty gummies
items.typicalAmount: usually 1 to 2.5 g collagen per serving
items.evidence: Same ingredient as collagen powder at a fraction of the dose and several times the price per gram.
items.goalNotes: Dose under 5 g a day: Tier 2 (dose too low), which is nearly every drink and gummy. Overlap group 'collagen'.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: There's about 2 g of collagen in each of these. The trials that found anything used 10. Same ingredient as the powder, one fifth of the dose, twice the price. $40 a month back.
items.factCheckNotes: Confirm the evidence claim in the 'what the studies found' column against one independent source.

items.name: Hair growth gummies (biotin blends)
items.evidence: Biotin, plus a multivitamin's worth of everything else. No hair effect without a deficiency, and deficiency is rare.
items.goalNotes: Tier 2 (tested, found nothing). Overlap group 'daily multivitamin'. Safety note as biotin.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.safety: Tell your doctor you take biotin before any blood test.
items.dayOne: Unless you're deficient, which almost nobody is, these don't grow hair. And the biotin in them can throw off blood tests. $30 a month back.
items.factCheckNotes: Confirm the evidence claim in the 'what the studies found' column against one independent source.

items.name: Sunscreen (daily SPF 30+)
items.evidence: The single best-supported skincare product there is for wrinkles and skin cancer. Nothing else on the shelf comes close.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 keep. Never routed for dropping.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: If you only keep one thing on this list, keep this one. A ring can't see it, and it doesn't matter; the evidence is as strong as evidence gets.

items.name: Retinol / retinoid (nightly)
items.evidence: The best-supported active for wrinkles and acne. Prescription tretinoin is stronger than over-the-counter retinol; both work with consistent use over months.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3 keep, with skin rating. Prescription: Protected. Overlap group 'exfoliants' if paired with an acid on the same night.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.safety: Not in pregnancy. Sun protection is required alongside.
items.dayOne: Well proven, and we can't see it, so a weekly skin rating is the honest way to watch it. Keep.

items.name: Vitamin C serum
items.lowestDoseText: form matters: L-ascorbic acid 10 to 20% in air-tight, opaque packaging
items.evidence: Decent evidence for L-ascorbic acid at 10 to 20% in the right packaging. Cheaper 'vitamin C' products using unstable forms or clear bottles have mostly oxidised before they reach your face.
items.goalNotes: form = L-ascorbic acid 10 to 20% in opaque packaging: Tier 3 with skin rating. form = other or unknown, or the product has turned orange: Tier 2 (form not absorbed).
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: If the bottle is clear or the serum has gone orange, the vitamin C is already gone. If it's a proper L-ascorbic acid formula, keep it and rate your skin weekly. That's $60 a month riding on the packaging.

items.name: Retinol or retinoid plus exfoliating acid on the same nights
items.evidence: Using both on the same night adds irritation, not results. Alternating nights gives the same benefit with less redness.
items.goalNotes: Overlap group 'exfoliants'. Same-night use: Tier 2 (overlaps with something else): alternate nights, or drop the acid.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: These two on the same night are fighting each other, and your skin is where the fight happens. Alternate nights and you get the same result with less redness. If you'd rather simplify, the acid is the one to drop.
items.factCheckNotes: Confirm the evidence claim in the 'what the studies found' column against one independent source.

items.name: Two exfoliants (scrub plus acid, or two acids)
items.evidence: One exfoliant is enough. Two is irritation.
items.goalNotes: Overlap group 'exfoliants'.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: One of these is doing the job and the other is doing damage. Keep the acid, drop the scrub. $25 a month back and calmer skin.
items.factCheckNotes: Confirm the evidence claim in the 'what the studies found' column against one independent source.

items.name: Toner (hydrating or balancing)
items.evidence: Modern cleansers don't leave skin needing 'rebalancing'. A hydrating toner does what the serum after it already does.
items.goalNotes: Overlap group 'hydrating layers': with a serum and a moisturiser in the routine, the toner is the drop.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: This step made sense with the harsh soaps of forty years ago. With a gentle cleanser and a serum, it's doing the serum's job for a second time. $25 a month back and one fewer bottle.
items.factCheckNotes: Confirm the evidence claim in the 'what the studies found' column against one independent source.

items.name: Multiple hydrating serums (two hyaluronic acid products)
items.evidence: One hyaluronic acid product hydrates. A second one is the same ingredient again.
items.goalNotes: Overlap group 'hydrating layers'.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Two bottles of the same ingredient. Keep the one you like the feel of. $50 a month back.
items.factCheckNotes: Confirm the evidence claim in the 'what the studies found' column against one independent source.

items.name: Eye cream (when you already use a moisturiser)
items.evidence: Most eye creams are the same formula as the brand's moisturiser in a smaller jar at a higher price per gram. The exceptions contain something the moisturiser doesn't (caffeine, retinol).
items.goalNotes: Overlap group 'hydrating layers'. Contains an active the moisturiser lacks: Tier 3. Otherwise Tier 2 (overlaps with something else).
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Read both labels. If the eye cream has an ingredient your moisturiser doesn't, keep it. If it's the same list in a smaller jar, that's $45 a month for the jar.
items.factCheckNotes: Confirm the evidence claim in the 'what the studies found' column against one independent source.

items.name: Facial plus at-home LED plus microcurrent (all three)
items.evidence: The LED has some evidence. The facial is short-term. Microcurrent has almost none. Running all three is paying three times for one visible result.
items.goalNotes: Overlap group 'professional skin treatments'. Devices unused in 30 days: Tier 2 (not being used). All in use: shown together with total cost; the person picks one.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Three things, one face, and only the LED has real evidence behind it. Pick one. If it's the facials, that's fine; just know the devices are then in a drawer costing $60 a month between them.
items.factCheckNotes: Confirm the evidence claim in the 'what the studies found' column against one independent source.

items.name: Microcurrent device (NuFace)
items.evidence: Almost no independent evidence. Any lift is temporary.
items.goalNotes: last used over 30 days ago: Tier 2 (not being used). Otherwise Tier 3 with skin rating. Overlap group 'at-home skin devices'.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Any lift from this is temporary, and the studies are the company's. If you use it and like it, that's a real reason. If it's in a drawer, it comes off the count.

items.name: Gua sha / ice roller
items.evidence: Temporary de-puffing, which is real and lasts hours. Nothing lasting.
items.goalNotes: Tier 3, free and harmless. Overlap group 'at-home skin devices'.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Costs nothing, feels nice, and the de-puffing is real for a few hours. Keep it if it's yours.

items.name: Cold plunge / ice bath tub (owned)
items.metricText: Overnight HRV; time to fall asleep
items.testDesign: 3 days on, 3 days off, for 14 days
items.evidence: As cold plunge.
items.goalNotes: last used over 30 days ago: Tier 2 (not being used). Otherwise as cold plunge (effect too small, can run anyway). Overlap group 'heat and cold'.
items.question: When did you last use it?
items.answerOptionsText: This week · this month · 1 to 3 months ago · longer · can't remember. 'Can't remember' is treated as 'longer'.
items.ruleText: unused for 30 days → Tier 2 (not being used). Otherwise as cold plunge.
items.dayOne: It's in the garage. When did you last get in it? If the answer is 'a while', that's the verdict, and no experiment is needed.

items.name: Unlisted device you haven't used in 30 days
items.evidence: The graveyard row. Anything typed in that isn't in the table and hasn't been used in a month.
items.goalNotes: last used over 30 days ago: Tier 2 (not being used). Otherwise Tier 3, untested.
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: You bought it, you tried it, and it's been in a drawer since spring. That's a verdict you reached on your own. It comes off the count, and if it has a resale value, that's the only number left.
items.factCheckNotes: Confirm the evidence claim in the 'what the studies found' column against one independent source.

items.name: Unlisted subscription you're still paying for
items.evidence: The auto-renew row. Anything billing monthly that the person hasn't used in 30 days.
items.goalNotes: still paying AND last used over 30 days ago: Tier 2 (not being used).
items.question: (no question)
items.answerOptionsText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.ruleText: Routes on the item name alone.
items.dayOne: Still billing, last used over a month ago. That's the whole verdict. Cancel it, and resubscribe the week you want it back.
items.factCheckNotes: Confirm the evidence claim in the 'what the studies found' column against one independent source.

metrics.name: Total sleep
metrics.description: How long you were asleep in total
metrics.drivers: Caffeine timing, alcohol, late fluids, a regular wake time, screens
metrics.notes: The most reliable number across devices. Default for any 'sleep' goal unless the row names another.

metrics.name: Time to fall asleep
metrics.drivers: Hot bath, melatonin, caffeine, screens, evening exercise, a worry list
metrics.notes: Devices guess when lights went out, so this is noisier on Apple and Garmin. Ignore nights over 60 minutes as one-offs.

metrics.name: Deep sleep
metrics.drivers: Alcohol (less, late in the night), room temperature, exercise
metrics.notes: Consumer sleep-stage numbers agree with a lab sleep study only about 60 to 70% of the time. A rough guide.

metrics.name: REM sleep
metrics.notes: Same rough-guide warning. Stopping alcohol or cannabis causes extra REM for a few nights, which confuses on/off tests.

metrics.name: Time awake during the night
metrics.description: Minutes awake after first falling asleep
metrics.drivers: Fluids after 8pm, alcohol, noise, light, pets, partner, kids
metrics.notes: Leave out any night marked 'kids woke me'.

metrics.name: Share of time in bed asleep
metrics.description: Asleep minutes divided by minutes in bed
metrics.drivers: A regular wake time, blackout, earplugs, temperature
metrics.notes: Can't go above 100, so little room to improve above about 92%.

metrics.name: Overnight HRV
metrics.description: The recovery number: how rested and unstrained your body is
metrics.personalSwingText: about 12 ms (about 20% of the person's average)
metrics.drivers: Alcohol (down 10 to 25%), late training, illness, slow breathing (up), sauna
metrics.notes: Most sensitive to alcohol and stress. The swing grows with the average, so compare in proportion. Apple Watch only samples now and then.

metrics.name: Resting heart rate
metrics.drivers: Alcohol (up), late meal (up), illness, stimulants, fitness (down over weeks)
metrics.notes: Very steady, so small changes stand out. Shifts 1 to 2 bpm across the menstrual cycle; note cycle phase where the person opts in.

metrics.name: Breathing rate
metrics.drivers: Illness, alcohol, nasal strips, air quality

metrics.name: Skin temperature
metrics.description: How far tonight is from your own normal
metrics.drivers: Alcohol, late meal, illness, room temperature, cycle phase
metrics.notes: Part of the alcohol 'signature' the app can spot. Leave out of tests where the cycle would confuse it.

metrics.name: Steps / activity
metrics.notes: Defines 'on' days for walking tests; flags days that shouldn't count.

metrics.name: Workouts (with start time)
metrics.description: When and how hard you trained
metrics.notes: This is how 'training after 7pm' can be read from history with no tagging at all.

goals.name: sleep (general)
goals.notes: Unless the row names a more specific number, total sleep is the default. It's the most reliable across devices.

goals.name: falling asleep
goals.notes: For anything taken or done in the hour before bed.

goals.name: deep sleep
goals.notes: Treat consumer sleep-stage numbers as a rough guide.

goals.name: recovery / stress / HRV
goals.notes: The most sensitive number to alcohol and stress. Compare in proportion to the person's average.

goals.name: energy
goals.metricText: Resting heart rate plus total sleep
goals.notes: A wearable can't see energy directly. If the person means 'how I feel', use the daily rating instead.

goals.name: focus / memory
goals.notes: Not visible to a wearable. Daily one-tap rating.

goals.name: mood / anxiety
goals.notes: Not visible. Daily one-tap rating. Diagnosed condition means Protected.

goals.name: skin / hair
goals.notes: Not visible. Daily one-tap rating over 8 weeks.

goals.name: gut / bloating
goals.notes: Not visible. Daily one-tap rating over 4 weeks.

goals.name: weight
goals.notes: Not a wearable number and not a two-week question. Shown as untestable here; the person's scale is the test.

goals.name: immunity
goals.notes: Not testable on one person in any reasonable time. Evidence shown, no test offered.

goals.name: longevity / general health
goals.notes: Not testable on one person, ever. Said plainly on day one; evidence and cost shown.

goals.name: testosterone / hormones
goals.notes: A blood test and a clinician. Never routed.

overlapGroups.name: fitness memberships
overlapGroups.ruleText: Two or more → show both with visits per month and cost per visit; the one used less becomes Tier 2 (overlaps with something else). A fitness app alongside a gym they attend is fine; alongside a gym they don't attend, both are flagged.

overlapGroups.name: heat and cold
overlapGroups.ruleText: Owns a sauna or plunge AND pays for a studio that offers the same → the studio is Tier 2 (overlaps with something else). Two studios → the one used less.

overlapGroups.name: massage
overlapGroups.ruleText: Membership plus separate massages → the membership's banked credits are checked first. Massage gun plus boots plus membership → verdict shows all three and their total; nothing is auto-dropped, since each feels different.

overlapGroups.name: meditation apps
overlapGroups.ruleText: Two → Tier 2 (overlaps with something else) for the one opened less in the last 30 days.

overlapGroups.name: wearables
overlapGroups.ruleText: Two wearables → Tier 2 for the one they'd rather not wear.

overlapGroups.name: wake-up light
overlapGroups.ruleText: A light box plus a sunrise alarm plus morning sunlight → the two devices overlap with the free one; shown, not auto-dropped.

overlapGroups.name: daily multivitamin
overlapGroups.ruleText: Multivitamin or greens powder PLUS a separate B12, D, zinc, C or K2 → the separates are Tier 2 (overlaps with something else) unless doctor-sourced (Protected) or the multi's dose is under the studied amount for that one.

overlapGroups.name: omega-3
overlapGroups.ruleText: Two or more → keep the fish oil, the others are Tier 2 (overlaps with something else).

overlapGroups.name: collagen
overlapGroups.ruleText: Collagen powder plus bone broth or collagen drinks → the second is Tier 2 (overlaps with something else). Powder wins on dose.

overlapGroups.name: caffeine before training
overlapGroups.ruleText: Pre-workout AND coffee within an hour of each other → verdict shows the combined caffeine; pre-workout becomes Tier 2 (overlaps with something else) since the coffee is the same drug for less.

overlapGroups.name: sleep aids
overlapGroups.ruleText: Three or more sleep aids → shown together with the total cost and the line 'you take {n} things for sleep and your sleep hasn't changed since {month}'. Melatonin plus sleep gummies → the gummies are Tier 2 (overlaps with something else).

overlapGroups.name: electrolytes
overlapGroups.ruleText: Both → the sports drink is Tier 2 (overlaps with something else).

overlapGroups.name: magnesium
overlapGroups.ruleText: Two or more magnesium products → keep one, the rest are Tier 2 (overlaps with something else).

overlapGroups.name: bloodwork
overlapGroups.ruleText: Both → the subscription is Tier 2 (overlaps with something else) unless it tests something the physical doesn't (ferritin, vitamin D are usually the reasons to keep it).

overlapGroups.name: professional skin treatments
overlapGroups.ruleText: Facials plus two or more at-home skin devices → the devices used least in 30 days are Tier 2 (not being used); if all used, shown together with total cost, pick one.

overlapGroups.name: exfoliants
overlapGroups.ruleText: Any two exfoliating steps in one routine → Tier 2 (overlaps with something else): alternate nights or drop one.

overlapGroups.name: hydrating layers
overlapGroups.ruleText: Toner plus serum plus moisturiser all doing 'hydration' → the toner is Tier 2 (overlaps with something else); a second hyaluronic serum is Tier 2; eye cream is Tier 2 unless it has an ingredient the moisturiser lacks.

overlapGroups.name: at-home skin devices
overlapGroups.ruleText: Two or more, each used less than weekly → Tier 2 (not being used) for the unused ones.

followUpQuestions.wording: Which form, and how much a day?
followUpQuestions.answerFormat: Form chips specific to the item, plus a number box with the unit prefilled. The label on the bottle answers both; we say so.

followUpQuestions.wording: How many times in the last 30 days?
followUpQuestions.answerFormat: 0 · 1 to 3 · 4 to 7 · 8 or more. For memberships, the app can prefill this from calendar or check-in data where connected.
Before noon · 12 to 2pm · 2 to 5pm · after 5pm (item-specific variants below). For workouts this is read from the wearable and not asked.

followUpQuestions.wording: How many nights a week, usually?
followUpQuestions.answerFormat: 0 · 1 to 2 · 3 to 4 · 5 or more. Asked plainly, no comment, no follow-up.

followUpQuestions.wording: When did you last use it?
followUpQuestions.answerFormat: This week · this month · 1 to 3 months ago · longer · can't remember. 'Can't remember' is treated as 'longer'.
Yes · no · not sure. Prefilled from the subscriptions list where the person connected one.
Fires on its own when two or more items from the same overlap group are both in the inventory. The person is shown both and asked which one they'd keep.
Routes on the item name alone.

verdictTemplates.name: Tier 1, kept
verdictTemplates.template: {item}: {number} was {change} better on the days you did it, against your normal swing of {swing}. That's real, and it's yours. Kept.
verdictTemplates.example: Morning walk: your overnight HRV was 6 points higher on the days you walked, against your normal swing of 3. That's real, and it's yours. Kept.

verdictTemplates.name: Tier 1, dropped
verdictTemplates.template: {item}: {number} was {change} worse on the days you did it, outside your normal swing of {swing}. {months} months in{source_clause}. Dropped, and {cost} a month back.
verdictTemplates.example: Training after 7pm: your total sleep was 41 minutes shorter on the nights you trained late, outside your normal swing of 30. Fourteen months in, and you'd never had a way to check. Dropped.

verdictTemplates.name: Tier 1, inconclusive
verdictTemplates.template: {item}: {change} on {number}, inside your normal swing of {swing}. At this dose, your body didn't show a change we could detect. That's a real answer, not a failed one. Your call whether it stays. It costs {cost} a month.
verdictTemplates.example: Melatonin: 3 minutes faster to fall asleep, inside your normal swing of 10. At this dose, your body didn't show a change we could detect. That's a real answer, not a failed one. Your call whether it stays. It costs $10 a month.

verdictTemplates.name: Tier 1, day-one hypothesis from history
verdictTemplates.template: {item}: on the {n_on} nights in the last {months} months when you {did it}, {number} was {change} {better/worse} than the other {n_off} nights. That's a pattern, not proof yet; other things differed on those nights too. Want to test it properly?
verdictTemplates.example: Training after 7pm: on the 22 nights in the last six months when you trained late, your total sleep was 34 minutes shorter than the other 140 nights. That's a pattern, not proof yet; other things differed on those nights too. Want to test it properly?

verdictTemplates.name: Tier 1, observe-only (morning after)
verdictTemplates.template: Last night: {what}. {number} came in {change} under your usual, and you were awake {awake} minutes more than normal. That's one {what}-night logged. {remaining} to go.
verdictTemplates.example: Last night: two drinks. Your HRV came in 19 points under your usual, and you were awake 34 minutes more than normal. That's one drinking night logged. Twelve to go.

verdictTemplates.name: Tier 1, slow (can't run yet)
verdictTemplates.template: {item}: this works over weeks, not nights, so a two-week on/off test would be unfair to it. What the trials found: {evidence}. We've put it in the queue for a longer test.
verdictTemplates.example: Ashwagandha: this works over weeks, not nights, so a two-week on/off test would be unfair to it. What the trials found: people said they felt less stressed after 6 to 8 weeks. We've put it in the queue for a longer test.

verdictTemplates.name: Tier 3, effect too small to see (new in v3)
verdictTemplates.template: {hook} Even when it works, the studies found a change of about {fraction} of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs. If you'd still like to run the test, you can, knowing that going in.
verdictTemplates.example: Magnesium glycinate: even in the studies where it worked, the change was a few minutes, mostly in people who were low in magnesium. Even when it works, the studies found a change of about a third of one night's normal swing, so a two-week test would very likely come back inconclusive. We'll show you what the trials found and what it costs. If you'd still like to run the test, you can, knowing that going in.

verdictTemplates.name: Tier 2, dose too low
verdictTemplates.template: {item}: the amount you're taking ({dose}) is below what the studies used ({threshold}). Nothing about you is the problem; the amount is. {cost} a month back, or step up to the studied amount and we'll test it properly.
verdictTemplates.example: Krill oil: the amount you're taking (500 mg) is below what the studies used (1 g of EPA and DHA). Nothing about you is the problem; the amount is. $30 a month back, or step up to the studied amount and we'll test it properly.

verdictTemplates.name: Tier 2, form not absorbed
verdictTemplates.template: {item}: this version ({form}) isn't absorbed well enough to do what you bought it for. Same ingredient, different version, and it becomes testable. {cost} a month back either way.
verdictTemplates.example: Magnesium oxide: this version isn't absorbed well enough to do what you bought it for. Same ingredient as glycinate, and that one can be tested. $8 a month back either way.

verdictTemplates.name: Tier 2, tested and found nothing
verdictTemplates.template: {item}: this has been tested properly, more than once, and it didn't do what it's sold for. You did the reasonable thing with the information you had. {months} months in{source_clause}. {cost} a month back.
verdictTemplates.example: Ginkgo: this has been tested properly, more than once, and it didn't do what it's sold for. You did the reasonable thing with the information you had. Two years in, on a friend's word. $15 a month back.

verdictTemplates.name: Tier 2, no way it could work
verdictTemplates.template: {item}: there's no known way for this to do what it claims, and no study says otherwise. If it's part of a routine you like, keep the routine. The {cost} is the only thing on trial.
verdictTemplates.example: Salt lamp: there's no known way for this to do what it claims, and no study says otherwise. It's a nice lamp. Keep the lamp.

verdictTemplates.name: Tier 2, duplicate
verdictTemplates.template: {item} and {other} do the same job. Keep the one you like; the other {cost} a month can go.
verdictTemplates.example: Oura and WHOOP do the same job. Keep the one you like; the other $30 a month can go.

verdictTemplates.name: Tier 3, with a daily rating offered
verdictTemplates.template: {item}: we can't see this in your data, and we won't pretend to. It costs {annual} a year. What the studies found: {evidence}. If you want an answer, a one-tap {goal} rating each day for {weeks} weeks is the honest way to get one.
verdictTemplates.example: Collagen: we can't see this in your data, and we won't pretend to. It costs $420 a year. What the studies found: small skin and joint improvements at 10 g a day after two months. If you want an answer, a one-tap skin rating each day for eight weeks is the honest way to get one.

verdictTemplates.name: Tier 3, keep (strong evidence)
verdictTemplates.template: {item}: a ring can't see this, and the evidence is strong anyway. Keep. Nothing to test here.
verdictTemplates.example: Creatine: a ring can't see this, and the evidence is strong anyway. If you lift, keep. Nothing to test here.

verdictTemplates.name: Tier 3, can't test (no specific goal)
verdictTemplates.template: {item}: you're taking this for general health, which is a real reason and not one a wearable can check. {annual} a year. We'll leave it in your count and out of your experiments.
verdictTemplates.example: Multivitamin: you're taking this for general health, which is a real reason and not one a wearable can check. $180 a year. We'll leave it in your count and out of your experiments.

verdictTemplates.name: Tier 3, free and harmless
verdictTemplates.template: {item}: costs nothing, can't be measured, and if it's yours, it's yours.
verdictTemplates.example: Gratitude journal: costs nothing, can't be measured, and if it's yours, it's yours.

verdictTemplates.name: Protected
verdictTemplates.template: {item}: this came from your clinician, so we don't rate it, test it, or suggest stopping it. It stays in your count only if you want it there.
verdictTemplates.example: Iron: this came from your blood test, so we don't rate it, test it, or suggest stopping it. It stays in your count only if you want it there.

toneRules.allowedPhrasesText: your call, yours, back (as in '$22 a month back'), kept, dropped, inconclusive, a real answer, we can't see it, what the studies found, your normal swing, your number, the night, the day, worth it, knowing that going in

rules.name: Name the effort before the number
rules.instruction: 'Eight months, every night' comes before the verdict. The verdict is about the item, never about their discipline.

rules.name: The source is context, not a punchline
rules.instruction: 'Started from a reel' is said once, in the past tense, and the sentence moves on. Never 'you fell for'.

rules.name: Tier 3 is never 'drop'
rules.instruction: 'We can't see it, here's the cost, here's the evidence, your call.' Several Tier 3 verdicts say keep.

rules.name: Tier 2 is about the dose or the study, never the person
rules.instruction: 'The amount is the problem, not you.' They acted sensibly on what they knew. Say so when it's true.

rules.name: Show the number, never the word 'wasted'
rules.instruction: Money appears as a plain figure and a plain 'back'.

rules.name: Free and enjoyed means keep
rules.instruction: If it costs nothing, does no harm, and they like it, the verdict says keep, whatever the number.

rules.name: Protected gets one sentence and no opinion
rules.instruction: Acknowledged and left alone. No evidence summary, no cost framing, no nudge.

rules.name: Safety notes are short, plain, and point to a person
rules.instruction: 'Ask a clinician.' One sentence, no alarm, then stop.

rules.name: Inconclusive gets its own respect
rules.instruction: 'Your body didn't show a change we could detect at this dose. That's a real answer.'

rules.name: Too-small-to-see gets told up front
rules.instruction: When the likely effect is under the gate, say so on day one, and let them run it anyway if they want. Never set up a test that's built to fail and then call the result inconclusive.

rules.name: Report what happened, not what they are
rules.instruction: 'Your HRV was 18 points lower after the drinks' is about the night. 'Your recovery is poor' is about the person. Always the first kind.

rules.name: Every off-plan night gets a normal next morning
rules.instruction: No red, no 'strain' warnings, no 'you should'. The number is shown, the cause is named, the day moves on.

rules.name: Their choice is the point, not the problem
rules.instruction: Every verdict ends with the decision in their hands. No 'should', 'need to', or 'must'.

rules.name: No exclamation marks, no 'great news'
rules.instruction: Plain sentences. A calm friend who happens to have read the studies.

rules.name: Second person, active voice, under 60 words
rules.instruction: Addressed to 'you', says what happened, stops. (Gated verdicts are allowed up to 60 because they carry an extra promise.)

rules.name: Never a health claim
rules.instruction: We describe what a habit did to a number, or what studies found about a habit. Never what a substance does to a condition. Never 'fix', 'cure', 'treat', 'prevent'.

A2.value: Built 20 September 2026 for Distill. The spreadsheet is the source of truth; a browsable copy is published as an artifact.

A4.value: What this file is, in one paragraph

A5.value: When someone finishes telling the app what they take, buy and do, every item gets looked up here. The row says what kind of thing it is, whether a ring or watch can see its effect, how big that effect is likely to be, what the studies found, and the exact sentence the person should read about it on day one. This table is the product's brain and its voice at the same time.

A6.value: You never ask the person which tier something is in. The tier comes out of this table plus their own answers (how much they take, what for, where the idea came from). The order the app checks things in is written out below.

A7.value: Nothing in here diagnoses, treats or prevents anything. Every sentence is about a habit, a dose, or a study. Never about a condition.

A10.value: The table routes on answers, not just names

B10.value: Five new columns per row. 'Follow-up question' says which question fires for the item (dose and form, frequency, clock time, nights a week, last used, still paying, or an automatic overlap check). 'Rule that flips the tier' is the exact threshold, written as a rule the engine can run: for magnesium, 'form = oxide or spray → form not absorbed; dose under 200 mg elemental → dose too low'. Magnesium glycinate at 400 mg and magnesium oxide at 100 mg are now the same row with two different outcomes, which is the whole point. Rows that need no question say 'none' and route as before.

B11.value: The day-one drops screen is generated from Tier 2, and Tier 2 is generated almost entirely from these answers. Without the follow-up questions, almost nothing lands in Tier 2 and that screen is empty. With them, a typical stack produces several drops on day one. See the Worked Example sheet.

A12.value: Two new reasons for a day-one drop

B12.value: 'Not being used' (a device in a drawer, a membership with banked credits, an app still billing) and 'overlaps with something else' (two gym memberships, a studio that duplicates a plunge at home, a toner doing the serum's job, collagen gummies next to collagen powder). Both use the same logic as the supplement drops: no test needed, drop it now. The dollar amounts are much larger, because services cost more than powders.

A13.value: The target person changed, and the table followed

B13.value: The person with thirty bottles was the old target. The new one is the premium-gym member who spends on services, classes, treatments and skincare, and wants to look and feel good. That person might own two supplements, so the 'cut at least five things in 60 days' promise can't be kept from dose failures alone. Thirty-four new rows cover memberships, class packs, recovery studios, massage memberships, meal services, apps, and a skincare section, plus 19 overlap groups (Overlap Groups sheet).

B14.value: Sunscreen and retinoids get a 'keep' with the strongest evidence in the file. Toners, second hyaluronic serums, most eye creams, doubled exfoliants and oxidised vitamin C serums are day-one drops. Every skincare verdict is about a product, never about a person's skin.

B15.value: The separate oxide row is gone; the form is now an answer to the magnesium question. Threonate and the spray stay separate because they're different products with different claims.

B18.value: Every row a wearable can see now has a number: how big the effect is likely to be, in units of one person's normal night-to-night swing. Below 0.8, a two-week test would usually come back inconclusive, so those rows get the honest Tier 3 treatment instead of a test that's set up to fail. The table used to send 81 rows to Tier 1; after the gate it's a much shorter list, and almost all of it is timing and behaviour, not supplements. That is a real finding about the product: the testable core is what people do, not what they swallow.

B19.value: Gated rows still let the person choose to run the test, told up front what to expect. Their choice is the point of the product; we just stop pretending a small effect is likely to show.

B20.value: A new column says whether the app can learn about an item from the person's existing wearable data before any test: workouts and wake times are recorded automatically; alcohol, caffeine and supplements only if they've been tagging them in Oura or WHOOP; and alcohol nights have a recognisable pattern (HRV down, resting heart rate up, temperature up, all together) that the app can flag for them to confirm. This is how the day-one 'hypotheses' get made, and it's why the morning-after-drinks screen logs the night rather than assigning it.

B21.value: Some items must never be assigned as an 'on' day: alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, energy drinks, fat burners. The app only records those when they happen, and may assign 'off' days. We never tell anyone to drink.

B22.value: Every Tier 2 row, and every row with a specific number in it, now carries a note saying exactly what to check and where to look. That's 90-odd rows, up from 2. Tier 2 rows tell someone to stop paying for something, so they are the exposure.

B23.value: Two double-parenthesis typos. The sauna habit row no longer carries the membership's cost. A stable key column for the engine. Cost per year as a live formula. A goal-to-number map so the routing has a defined metric for every goal.

A25.value: The four tiers, in plain words

B26.value: A wearable can see it, it acts within hours, and the likely effect is big enough to show in two weeks. Three days on, three off, repeat. One number chosen before the start. One word at the end: kept, dropped, or inconclusive, always with the actual number.

B27.value: The answer is already known on day one. Five reasons: the dose is too low, the form isn't absorbed, it's been tested properly and found to do nothing, there's no known way it could work, or it duplicates something they already have. The person sees the money back immediately.

B28.value: Either a wearable is blind to it, or the likely effect is too small to see in two weeks. We say which. We show the cost per year and what the studies found, and offer a one-tap daily rating for things you'd feel rather than measure. Tier 3 is NOT 'drop': creatine, fibre, strength training and a personal trainer are Tier 3 and get a 'keep'.

B29.value: Anything from a doctor, a blood test, a prescription, a hormone, or tied to a diagnosed condition. Never rated, tested, or suggested for dropping. In the count only if they want it there.

A31.value: The order the app checks things (top to bottom, first match wins)

B32.value: Doctor or blood test source, prescription, hormone, clinical service, or a diagnosed condition named for it. Stop.

B33.value: Attach it. A few redirect to Protected (mouth tape with possible sleep apnoea; 5-HTP with an antidepressant).

B34.value: 'General health' or 'nothing specific' goes to Tier 3 as untestable, cost shown.

B35.value: Run the row's follow-up question. Dose below the floor, form not absorbed, evidence grade N for the goal, no way it could work: Tier 2 with the reason. Then the usage checks: last used over 30 days ago, or still paying and not using: Tier 2 (not being used). Then the overlap check: two or more items from the same overlap group: Tier 2 (overlaps with something else) for the one used less. The person is always shown both and asked which they'd keep.

A36.value: 5. Wearable can see it, acts fast, effect at least 0.8?

B36.value: Tier 1. Order the person's Tier 1 list by expected effect, largest first. Check the 'read from history' column: if the app already has weeks of on and off nights from tags or workouts, show that comparison as a day-one hypothesis before the test.

A37.value: 6. Wearable can see it, acts fast, effect under 0.8?

B37.value: Tier 3, 'effect too small to see in two weeks', with the option to run it anyway.

A38.value: 7. Wearable can see it but it's slow?

B38.value: Tier 1 in principle, queued. Never run 3-day blocks on it.

B39.value: Tier 3. Daily rating offered only for goals you'd feel rather than measure.

A41.value: How the effect numbers were made, and how much to trust them

A42.value: Each is the typical published effect for the row's main number, divided by a typical person's normal night-to-night swing for that number (see the 'Numbers we can watch' sheet). Where the effect depends on the person (a hot sleeper, a snorer, someone with night bathroom trips), the 'where the estimate comes from' column says what number to use instead. These are working estimates from the literature as I know it, not a meta-analysis, and every one of them is a fair target for the team to challenge. The gate at 0.8 is a judgement call: at 0.8, seven nights a side gives roughly a one-in-three chance of a clear answer; at 1.2 it's better than even.

B45.value: Hot bath or shower 1 to 2 hours before bed, 14 days. Same mechanism.

B49.value: Heaviest duvet already owned, 3 on and 3 off.

B50.value: No stand-in. The shop's 100-night trial is the test.

B51.value: One month at the studied dose, then the row's test.

B52.value: No stand-in and no evidence. The verdict is the annual cost.
