B55.value: A stable code for the engine. Doesn't change when the item is renamed.

B56.value: US retail estimate, prefilled in onboarding and editable. One-off devices are spread over 24 months. Per year is a live formula.

B58.value: Chosen before the test and never changed after.

A59.value: How fast it acts and clears

B59.value: fast = hours, so 3-day blocks work. slow = weeks, so they don't.

B60.value: How big the change is likely to be, in units of that person's normal night-to-night swing. 1.0 means 'about as big as a normal bad night versus a normal good night'.

A61.value: Chance of a clear answer in two weeks

B61.value: good (1.2 and up), fair (0.8 to 1.2), low (under 0.8), or not applicable.

A62.value: Tier / Tier after the effect gate

B62.value: The first is the row's natural tier. The second is what the engine actually uses, after the 0.8 gate and the slow-item queue.

A63.value: Can we read it from their history?

B65.value: A = well-run trials agree, measured properly. B = proper trials but small, mixed, or based on how people felt. C = a few small trials or studies that only watched people. D = stories, marketing, lab-dish or animal only. N = tested properly and found to do nothing.

B66.value: The actual sentence, in the product's voice. Read the Tone Guide and Emotional Positioning sheets before changing any.

A17.value: The test: two weeks of 3 on, 3 off. On-nights versus off-nights (usually 7 against 7; fewer if taps were missed, and a missed tap is 'unknown', never 'failed'). One question: is the difference bigger than this person's normal swing by enough that it would only happen by chance about 1 time in 20, in the direction we said before the start? Yes = kept or dropped. No = inconclusive. The number is shown either way.

A18.value: In practice: with 7 nights a side, the difference needs to be about one and a half times the swing to count reliably. That is why the Items sheet carries an expected-effect column and why rows under 0.8 are not sent to a two-week test by default. Alcohol on HRV and afternoon caffeine on total sleep are one to two swings, so they usually resolve. Magnesium on deep sleep is a fifth to a third of a swing, so it would almost always come back inconclusive, and the person is told that on day one instead.

A19.value: Nights that shouldn't count: the person can flag a night (ill, travelling, a child woke them, an unusually hard session) and it's left out. Weekend nights are spread evenly by starting the schedule on a Monday.

A20.value: Reading history first: for items the wearable already records (workouts, wake times, naps) or that the person has been tagging, the app can compare past on-nights and off-nights before any test. Treat that as a hypothesis, not a verdict: those nights weren't randomised, so other things differed too. The test confirms it.

A1.value: Emotional positioning: what the psychology research says, and what we do about it

A2.value: Full sources in Emotional-Positioning-Research.md next to this file.

A5.value: Every wearable app today is built on the same assumption: show people a bad number and they'll behave better. The research says the opposite happens more often than not. A bad number that points at the person makes them feel judged, and people who feel judged argue with the app, hide from it, or do the thing more. The ring goes in the drawer. That gap is psychological, not technical, and it's the positioning.

A7.value: Six findings, and what each one changes in the product

A8.value: 1. Feedback that points at the self makes performance worse

B8.value: Kluger and DeNisi (1996) pooled 607 studies and found over a third of feedback made people perform worse. Feedback aimed at the person ('your recovery is poor') hurts; feedback kept on the task ('sleep was 41 minutes shorter on those nights') helps. WHAT WE DO: every verdict is about the night and the habit, never the person. No score that describes you.

A9.value: 2. One slip plus guilt leads to a bigger slip

B9.value: The 'what-the-hell effect' (Polivy and Herman): once someone feels they've blown it, they abandon the whole plan. In drinkers, the guiltiest about last night drank MORE the next night (UCL, 2025). WHAT WE DO: the morning after an off-plan night is a normal morning. The number is shown, the cause named without comment, nothing is red, the experiment continues.

A10.value: 3. Being told what to do makes ambivalent people argue back

B10.value: Motivational interviewing's 'righting reflex': push one side and the person defends the other. Directive styles produce more drop-out. Health-app experiments find controlling language raises resistance and choice lowers it. WHAT WE DO: no 'should', ever. Every verdict ends with the decision in their hands. That now includes the gated rows: 'run it anyway' is offered, not withheld.

A11.value: 4. Self-compassion predicts healthier behaviour, not laziness

B11.value: Sirois, Kitner and Hirsch (2015), 15 samples, 3,252 people: people kinder to themselves after failing do MORE healthy things, because they aren't spending energy on shame. WHAT WE DO: lapses are expected. Missed taps are unknown, never failed. A reset protocol for bad weeks.

A12.value: 5. Praise the process, not the person, and the same for criticism

B12.value: Dweck: 'you worked hard' builds persistence, 'you're smart' makes people fragile. WHAT WE DO: 'Eight months, every night' comes before every verdict.

A13.value: 6. The tracker itself can become the problem

B13.value: Baron et al. (2017) named orthosomnia: people at sleep clinics with normal sleep and real anxiety from chasing a score. Epstein's work found apps punish lapses instead of designing for them. WHAT WE DO: no daily score, no dashboard, one line a day, verdicts every two weeks, an option to hide the wearable's own score.

B16.value: A red recovery of 31%. A strain warning. 'Alcohol had a significant negative impact.' A suggestion to take it easy. The person feels flamed for a nice evening, and has learned nothing they didn't know.
